## AI agents: should you hire them like employees?
URL : https://exec-ia.ai/perspective-agents-ia-recruter-comme-salarie-en.html

← All articles Blog • AI agents
AI agents: should you hire them
like employees?
Article developed from my LinkedIn post (09/10/2026) · Updated on October 12, 2026
Short version →
Leaders and managers: since March 2026, monday.com has offered Agentalent.ai, a platform to "hire" AI agents, complete with job description, trial period and "salary".
The detail that matters: a real person remains accountable for every agent.
Before you hire one, ask three leadership-team questions: which task to give it, which decisions it may never take, and who answers for its mistakes.
You run a company or a team, and your vendors keep talking about AI agents?
This year, you can "hire" one, almost like an employee.
This article helps you do it with method, and stay in control.
🎯 What is an AI agent?
An AI agent is software that takes action. It reads a request, checks your tools, drafts a reply, chases a client, updates a spreadsheet. An assistant waits for your question; an agent strings several steps together towards a goal you set.
That is what makes it useful. It is also why it needs a frame: an agent that acts can make mistakes while acting.
What is Agentalent.ai?
In March 2026, monday.com, the project-management software company, launched Agentalent.ai. It borrows the model of a recruitment agency and applies it to AI agents.
The process looks like hiring:
you describe the role in plain language;
the platform's team introduces a suitable agent;
the agent is set up on your tools in about a week;
you get two weeks to decide, with a full refund if it isn't a fit.
Pricing follows the same logic: one month of "salary" paid once, or that "salary" every month plus a 15% platform fee.
The detail that matters more than the price
The platform says it plainly: a real person on its team is responsible for every agent it lists, with a name and an email address. So even at an agent vendor, no agent works without a human in charge.
Why this is reaching SMEs
Major software vendors are building agents into the tools SMEs already use: email, business software, customer-relationship tools. Your teams will come across them, often without anyone deciding it. The real choice is which ones, and under whose authority.
What twenty years of onboarding taught me
In twenty years alongside senior executives, I prepared many arrivals: the job description, the system access, the one-month check-in. An AI agent deserves the same rigour. It touches your data, your clients, sometimes your cash.
🎯 Three leadership-team questions before hiring one:
Which task should it take on, precise and repetitive?
Which decisions remain off-limits?
Who on the leadership team answers for its mistakes?
In my article on CV screening, the conclusion was the same: a decision that affects a person stays human. An agent can prepare, follow up and sort. It does not decide alone on the fate of a client or an employee.
💬 In your company,
which task would you hand to an agent first?
Sources: Agentalent.ai, how it works and pricing; monday.com press release, 23 March 2026; Constellation Research, launch analysis; Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 50; GDPR, Article 22.
#EXECIA #ArtificialIntelligence #AIAgents #Governance #Leadership
Read the full articleabout 1,700 words→
Chatbot, automation, agent: what's the difference?
A chatbot answers questions. An automation runs the same scenario every time, step by step, like a recipe. An agent receives a goal and chooses its own steps: it looks up information, calls a tool, checks a result, tries again if needed.
That autonomy changes everything. A failing automation stops. A mistaken agent can carry on, confidently, in the wrong direction. That is why the question of who is in charge matters for an agent, and far less for a simple automation.
What the hiring metaphor gets right
It forces you to write a job description. Many AI projects fail because nobody defined the task: "help us with customer service" is not enough. "Answer order-tracking questions, and never grant a commercial gesture" is.
It requires a trial period, and therefore measurement. And it reminds you that every newcomer has a manager. These three habits are worth their weight in gold, and they cost nothing.
What it hides
An agent has no judgement, no loyalty, no intuition. It doesn't raise its hand when it doesn't know: it produces a plausible answer. It doesn't absorb company culture by watching colleagues. It does what its instructions and data allow, nothing more.
Above all, an agent is not an employee in the legal sense. It carries no liability of its own. When it processes personal data, your company remains the data controller. When it gets something wrong with a client, your company answers for it.
Writing an agent's job description
Six headings on a single page are enough:
the mission, in one sentence;
the authorised tasks, listed one by one;
the forbidden decisions, written down in black and white;
the tools and data it may access, kept to the strict minimum;
the threshold at which it hands over to a human;
the indicators that will show whether it does the job well.
This page works twice. It frames the vendor who sets up the agent. It also tells your teams what the agent does, and what it doesn't.
The trial period: what to measure
Two weeks go fast. Measure four things from day one:
the errors spotted by the person who reviews its work;
the time actually saved, not the time promised in the brochure;
the cases it passed to a human, and the ones it should have passed;
the reactions of clients or colleagues who dealt with it.
If nobody has time to review its work during the trial, the trial proves nothing. Plan that time before you sign.
Who manages the agent?
Name one person, by name. Give them time to review, correct and adjust the instructions. Above all, give them the authority to switch the agent off, without waiting for a committee, if something looks wrong.
In an SME, this manager is usually whoever runs the activity concerned: accounts for a payment-reminder agent, customer service for a reply agent. They don't need to be technical. They need to know the business.
What the law already says
Article 22 of the GDPR protects everyone against decisions based solely on automated processing when they significantly affect them. An agent that alone refuses a loan, a refund or a job application falls within that scope.
Since 2 August 2026, the AI Act also sets a transparency rule: people must know they are dealing with an AI, unless it is obvious. An agent that writes to your clients must therefore say what it is. And uses that touch recruitment or the management of employees fall under high-risk systems, with obligations from 2 December 2027.
The real price of an agent
The advertised "salary" is only part of the cost. According to Constellation Research, agents on Agentalent.ai started at around $2,000 a month at launch, with 17 agents available. That is an analyst's estimate, to be checked case by case.
Add your team's time to prepare data, write the job description, review the agent's work during the trial, then supervise it. An agent that saves ten hours a week but needs five hours of checking delivers half of what it promises.
Three tasks where an agent helps an SME
The best candidates are precise, repetitive and easy to check:
chasing unpaid invoices, with a message approved in advance;
sorting incoming requests and routing them to the right person;
preparing a briefing before a meeting: client history, recent exchanges, open points.
In all three cases, a mistake shows quickly and is easy to fix. It is the best way to learn how to work with an agent.
Three decisions never to hand over
Some decisions always keep a human face:
hiring, rejecting or dismissing a person;
granting an exceptional discount or an off-policy commercial gesture;
answering an angry client or a client in dispute.
The agent can prepare each of these decisions: gather the facts, draft a reply, flag the urgency. The decision itself belongs to someone who can explain it.
Signs that an agent is drifting
Four signals should alert its manager:
it gives different answers to the same question;
it acts outside its scope, even with good intentions;
clients ask to speak to a human more often than before;
nobody reviews its work any more, because "it works".
The last signal is the most dangerous. An agent that has been reliable for three months earns trust, and that is exactly when vigilance drops.
What I advise leaders
A five-step method, with no big budget:
start with a single task, precise and easy to check;
write the agent's job description on one page;
name its manager, with the time and authority to switch it off;
measure the two-week trial on four indicators;
review every quarter what it does, and what else it could take on.
Hiring an AI agent is not an IT project. It is an organisational decision, to be prepared like the arrival of a new colleague.
An AI agent can work fast and without rest. Every decision it prepares should still carry a person's name.
Valérie Mailland
Founder of EXEC'IA Consulting. 20+ years alongside executives, including 18 in executive coordination at McKinsey & Company. Follow me on LinkedIn →

## Buy-in matters more than the AI budget
URL : https://exec-ia.ai/perspective-budget-ia-adhesion-equipes-en.html

← All articles Blog • Buy-in
The AI budget is not the issue.
Buy-in is.
September 25, 2026 · Updated on October 1, 2026
Short version →
Business leaders: a generous AI budget does not guarantee that your teams will use the tool.
A 2026 Gallup study shows the gap: nearly one employee in two works for an organisation that has integrated AI, yet only 15% use it daily.
Three levers make the difference: explain before equipping, train on everyday uses, prove a concrete result on a small scope before scaling up.
You run a company and you have just approved an AI budget?
This piece is for you.
A generous budget, approved without discussion. Teams that do not move at the same pace. I have seen this scenario in executive committees, long before AI became the topic.
A July 2026 Gallup study confirms it: 47% of US employees say their organisation has integrated AI tools, yet only 15% of workers use AI daily. One in five does not even know whether their organisation has adopted it: the investment happened, the explanation did not always follow.
Among marketers, HubSpot saw the same pattern in 2025: 98% of companies planned to maintain or increase their AI investment, yet only half of their employees, 51%, actually wanted to use it.
The study covers marketers. I read it as a signal, not as a statistic that holds for every job. But the signal is clear: the budget is not the issue. Buy-in is.
🔑 Why does buy-in weigh more than budget?
Because a tool never changes an organisation on its own. Your teams decide every day whether to use it or work around it.
You can sign the best contract on the market: if nobody opens the tool on Monday morning, you have bought a licence, not a change.
Resistance almost never comes from the technology. It comes from the habits the tool is asked to replace.
A habit is years of gestures that work. You do not replace it with an announcement. You replace it with a better way of working that the team has tested for itself.
What does the gap between investment and willingness to use the tool reveal?
Two clocks run in parallel.
The first is the clock of the decision: a budget is approved in a few weeks, a tool is rolled out in a few months.
The second is the clock of habits: they change at the pace of the teams, not at the pace of the executive committee’s diary.
When these two clocks are not set together, the company pays for a use that does not exist yet. The dashboard says the tool is deployed. The field says it is opened now and then, then forgotten.
My advice: before talking budget, ask how long your teams will need to change their habits. It usually takes longer than the rollout.
Why is the budget spent a poor indicator?
Because it measures an intention, not a change. A budget spent proves that a decision was taken. It says nothing about what teams do differently on Monday morning compared with yesterday.
The right indicator is regular use: how many people use the tool each week, for which precise task, and what have they stopped doing by hand?
How do you measure buy-in, in practice?
Three questions are enough to start.
Who uses it every week, and for what?
Who tried it and gave up, and why?
Which task has really disappeared or become shorter?
These answers come from a twenty-minute conversation with a few team members, not from a satisfaction form. They give a truer picture than any login statistic.
Why does a team adopt a tool?
A team adopts a tool when it sees the benefit for itself, not only for the company. The gain must be felt in daily work: a shorter task, one less error, a file prepared faster.
When the benefit is only visible on a leadership dashboard, the tool is experienced as an extra burden. The first job is therefore to translate the expected benefit into the language of the people who will use it.
Which forms of resistance come up most often?
Three come back.
1) The fear of getting it wrong, especially when the tool seems to leave no room for error.
2) The fear of being replaced, which is rarely said out loud.
3) The feeling that the tool adds a step instead of removing one.
Each one calls for its own answer: a right to try, a clear word from leadership about what will not change, and a demonstration on a real task rather than a catalogue example.
Why explain before equipping?
🎯 Which levers really make the difference?
Three, from the simplest to the most demanding.
1) Explain before equipping.
2) Train on real uses.
3) Prove early.
The why always comes before the tool. A team that understands what the tool changes in its daily work, and what it does not, adopts it more readily than a team that is simply told about a rollout.
Explaining takes one meeting. Not explaining costs months of silent resistance.
How do you train without overwhelming teams?
Start from everyday uses, not from the list of features. One hour on a task a person does every week is worth more than a full day of general demonstration.
When should the tool be extended to the whole organisation?
After proving a concrete result, early, on a limited scope. That result becomes the argument, in place of the promise. The rollout then reaches teams who have already seen what the tool delivers.
What should you do when a team works around the tool?
Start by understanding, before restating the rule. A workaround is almost never ill will. It reveals a need the tool does not cover, a step that is too heavy, or a habit nobody helped to change.
A team that works around a tool is telling you, without saying it, what it expects from it. That is valuable information, provided you gather it without hunting for culprits.
What role does the leader play in buy-in?
A role of demonstration more than of decision. A leader who uses the tool personally, who says what it is useful for and where it disappointed, gives teams permission to try and to say what does not work.
Conversely, a tool imposed without being used by those who impose it sends a message that contradicts the speech.
Which mistakes should you avoid in a rollout?
Four come back.
1) Deploying everywhere at once.
2) Training on the list of features.
3) Announcing without explaining the why.
4) Judging success by the budget spent rather than by real use.
Each has the same origin: treating the tool as a purchase to succeed rather than as a change of practice to support.
How do you run a thirty-day pilot?
Week one: choose a volunteer team and a task that recurs every week, then explain why.
Week two: train on that task only.
Week three: let the team use it and note what gets in the way.
Week four: measure the result and decide to continue, adjust or stop.
At the end of the month, the leader has something the budget alone never provided: proof, inside their own organisation, of what the tool brings or does not bring.
What role should line managers play?
A central one. They turn the decision into daily practice. A convinced manager sets the example, protects learning time and reports what gets in the way.
A manager who was not involved becomes, unintentionally, the first brake.
Before rolling out, it is worth holding a short session for these relays: what changes for them, what they will tell their teams, and whom they will turn to when a difficulty appears.
How do you know whether buy-in is growing?
Three concrete signs.
1) The same people come back to the tool from one week to the next.
2) They mention it unprompted when they describe their work.
3) They suggest new uses themselves.
Conversely, use concentrated on one or two people, or vanishing as soon as the coaching stops, signals surface-level buy-in. These signals are picked up by observation and conversation, with no extra measurement tool.
What should you tell a leader who wants to go fast?
Speed comes from buy-in, not from haste.
A fast rollout to a team that has not bought in costs time twice: once to install it, once to relaunch it. A short pilot with a visible result convinces faster than a communication plan.
The right timetable is one where each step proves something to the next team.
What role do the first users play?
The first convinced users are the best relays. Their feedback, in their own words, carries more weight than a presentation from leadership. Identify them early, give them a little time to go deeper, and let them show colleagues what works and what does not.
Take care not to turn them into isolated experts: their role is to share, not to carry the use alone for the whole team.
How do you keep momentum after launch?
A use that is no longer animated fades. Plan a short, regular meeting to share what worked, what got in the way and what each person tried. Fifteen minutes is enough, provided it actually happens.
Highlight a concrete result rather than a usage figure: a task shortened, a file delivered earlier. That is what other teams will remember.
Every team has its own rhythm, and comparing one team with another rarely helps. What matters is that each one can see, in its own work, what has changed since the tool arrived, and that someone listens when it says what still gets in the way. That listening is what keeps the tool alive after the launch effect has faded.
💬 And you, how do you measure
the gap between investment and buy-in?
Sources: HubSpot, “AI Trends for Marketers 2025”, a 2025 study of marketers worldwide; Gallup, “Organizational AI Adoption Jumps Six Points”, 20 July 2026.
#ArtificialIntelligence #Leadership #AITransformation #Governance #HubSpot #EXECIA
Read the full articleabout 3,000 words→
Four attitudes towards a new tool
In every team, reactions fall into roughly the same pattern. Spotting them lets you support each person in their own way, instead of giving everyone the same speech.
I often see four attitudes:
the enthusiasts, who have already tried it and want to go faster;
the cautious, who are waiting for concrete results;
the sceptics, who doubt the value and say so;
the worried, who fear for their job or their skills, often without saying it.
The enthusiasts become ambassadors, as long as they are not left on their own. The cautious are won over by proof. The sceptics deserve a hearing: they often spot real flaws. The worried first need reassurance about their future.
Age is not the issue
You often hear that younger people take to AI more easily. In practice, buy-in depends far more on perceived usefulness than on generation.
An experienced employee who saves an hour on a tedious task adopts the tool very quickly. A young employee who cannot see what it is for turns away from it. Reasoning by age leads to poor training choices, and sometimes to hurtful blunders.
Words that reassure, words that worry
The words of the announcement weigh more than you think. “Replace”, “automate jobs”, “productivity gains”: even with no bad intent, people hear them as a threat.
“Lighten”, “free up time for”, “help you to” often describe the same reality, but from the point of view of the person doing the work. Choosing your words is not window dressing: it means recognising that the person opposite has something to lose, and taking that seriously.
Protect learning time
Many rollouts fail for a very simple reason: teams are asked to learn a tool on top of their work, without being given the time.
Set aside a short, regular slot, for example one hour a week during the first month. It changes everything. That protected time also sends a message: for the company, learning is part of the job, not an extra effort to squeeze into the evening.
A shared library of good prompts
Every user ends up finding the wordings that work. If they stay in people’s heads, the company keeps relearning the same thing.
A shared library, kept simple, sorts these prompts by task: preparing meeting notes, rewording a letter, summarising a tender. Everyone draws on it and adds to it. Newcomers get started faster, and those who found the best practices get recognised.
Should you reward usage?
Recognise it, yes. Pay for it, no. A bonus tied to the number of logins pushes people to use the tool for the figure, not for the result, and it distorts the indicators leadership looks at.
The recognition that works best is often the simplest: mention a success in a meeting, make someone the go-to person, give them time to help their colleagues. What motivates people over time is being seen as useful.
How do you welcome newcomers?
By putting AI tools into the onboarding path, just like business software. A new employee who discovers in their first week the uses in place, the prompt library and the rules to follow picks up good habits straight away.
A buddy who is already comfortable with these tools speeds things up even more. The newcomer learns the team’s real uses, not just the ones in a manual.
Show internal successes
Nothing convinces like a colleague. An example from the team next door, with its figures and its limits, speaks louder than an international study or a vendor demo.
A short monthly share, five minutes in a meeting, where someone shows what the tool has brought them, gradually builds a culture. Show the trials that did not work too: they prove people are allowed to get it wrong.
The right to say it does not work
Buy-in is not obedience. A team that can say a tool does not suit them, without being suspected of bad will, gives you precious information.
Set up a simple channel for this feedback, and answer it. Teams see that their opinion counts, and leadership avoids pushing a tool nobody really uses.
What role for HR?
A supporting role, often underestimated. HR can bring AI uses into annual reviews, spot training needs and identify people who are struggling before they drop out.
They can also watch a sensitive point: when a tool saves time, what happens to that time?
If it only turns into extra workload, buy-in crumbles. If it goes into more interesting tasks, buy-in grows.
Remote teams?
The rules are the same, with one extra risk: isolation. Alone in front of a screen, an employee who gets stuck gives up faster, with no neighbour to ask.
Short video sessions, pairs who help each other and a written space where people can ask questions without fear of looking behind make up for most of that distance.
When the tool changes?
AI tools change constantly: a new interface, a new version, a feature moved or removed. Every change can break a habit that has barely formed, and wipe out the benefit of the first weeks.
The go-to person plays a key role here: they follow the updates, warn the team about what is changing, update the prompt library and, if needed, offer a short refresher. A change that is announced is absorbed in a few days. A change that is imposed can make people drop the tool.
What do you do about lasting refusal?
Start with a one-to-one conversation, with no pressure. A refusal that lasts often hides a precise reason: a bad first experience, a task the tool does not serve, a worry about the future of the job.
Often, the tool is not essential for everyone, and you can give it time. When it becomes essential, for example because a whole process depends on it, explain it clearly, give more support and set a realistic deadline. Forcing it rarely produces real buy-in.
How long before a use becomes a habit?
Usually several weeks of regular practice. The first days are curiosity. The habit forms when the tool is used for a real task, several times a week.
Two checkpoints help you follow this shift: after one month, to fix what gets in the way, and after three months, to check that the use holds once the launch buzz has faded.
A typical example
Take an SME of forty people that bought licences for everyone, with no result after three months. Rather than adding a general training course, leadership starts by listening: a short conversation with each team brings up unspoken worries and two uses that already work.
It protects one hour a week, builds a prompt library from those two uses and asks the people who found them to present them. Three months later, regular use has clearly grown, without spending a penny more. What was missing was not the tool. It was the way of supporting people.
What buy-in really takes
Consideration more than conviction. You do not win a team’s buy-in by explaining that the tool is good. You win it by showing that you understand what it changes for them.
A budget buys licences. Only the attention you pay to people makes them want to use them.
Valérie Mailland
Founder of EXEC'IA Consulting. 20+ years alongside executives, including 18 in executive coordination at McKinsey & Company. Follow me on LinkedIn →

An AI policy that its own leaders do not follow is no longer a policy.

## Chatbot: knowing when to hand over
URL : https://exec-ia.ai/perspective-chatbot-savoir-passer-la-main-en.html

← All articles Blog • Customer relations
Air France’s chatbot answers
a share of requests alone.
For the rest, it knows
when to hand over.
September 25, 2026 · Updated on October 1, 2026
Short version →
Business leaders, heads of customer service: Louis, Air France’s AI assistant, handles a share of customer requests on its own (according to the press). The rest it passes to a human, and the customer does not have to repeat everything.
To me, this figure does not show progress in AI. It shows the boundary Air France has learned to draw.
Three signals help you sense the limit before you cross it. Knowing when to hand over is still a human reflex.
You run a company and you wonder how far to trust a chatbot with your customer service?
This piece is for you.
Take Louis, Air France’s AI assistant. It merged several generations of specialised chatbots (baggage, travel inspiration, strikes and delays) into a single assistant, active on WhatsApp and Messenger.
🤝 What does that figure really say?
Today, according to the press, Louis handles a share of customer requests on its own. The rest goes to a human, and the customer does not need to ask everything again.
What strikes me about this figure?
It is not the AI that has progressed the most. It is the boundary Air France has learned to draw between the tool and the person.
This is not an isolated case. According to Salesforce, in 2025 customer service teams already hand an average of 30% of their cases to AI. They expect to reach 50% by 2027.
In other words, the boundary question is coming to almost every customer service team, SMEs included.
Automating a frequent request frees up time.
Knowing how to route the rest: that is the real skill.
Why does the handover matter as much as the automation?
Because your customers do not judge the technology. They judge their journey.
You can automate 30% of requests successfully and lose it all on a single failed handover: the one where the customer has to repeat everything to an adviser who knows nothing about the previous exchange.
A good handover passes on the context: what the customer asked, what the tool replied, what is left to solve. The adviser picks up the conversation where it stopped.
For the company, it is an organisational detail. For the customer, it is the whole difference between “someone is looking after me” and “I am starting from scratch”.
Which requests should never be automated end to end?
Those where the stakes are high or emotions run strong: a dispute, an emergency, a customer in difficulty, a decision that commits the company.
These requests are often few. But their effect on trust is huge.
For these cases, the best automation spots the situation and alerts a human fast.
What should you take from the Air France example?
The result does not come from how sophisticated the tool is. It comes from how clear the roles are.
The assistant handles what is frequent and simple. People handle what calls for judgement, listening or a decision.
This split moves: you revisit it as the tool improves and teams see what it does well.
What can be automated without risk?
Frequent, factual requests with a stable answer: the status of an order, a timetable, a known rule, a document to find.
The right answer depends neither on the customer’s mood nor on a judgement call.
That is where automation frees up the most time for your teams. It is also where a mistake costs the least.
How does a customer experience a failed handover?
As an admission: the company did not organise itself for them.
They repeat their problem, they wait, they switch channels. They remember that moment more vividly than all the answers that worked.
Trust is rarely lost over a single mistake. It is lost when people feel they are not being heard, especially when it is urgent.
How do you sense the limit before crossing it?
To me, three signals are enough.
1) The customer repeats the question.
2) They cannot find a way to reach a human.
3) The tone does not match how serious the request is.
Does the customer repeat the question before getting a useful answer?
When the same question keeps coming back, the tool is not meeting the real need. That is the first signal: the conversation needs to change hands.
Is there a simple option to reach a human?
If no clear option appears, customers feel trapped.
Good automation makes the way out to a person visible and immediate. A button, a sentence, a phone number: the form does not matter, as long as nobody has to hunt for it.
Does the tone adapt to how serious the request is?
The tone cannot stay the same for a trivial question and for an emergency. A staff strike does not call for the same register as a baggage question.
AI handles the volume. Recognising the right moment to hand over is still a human reflex.
Who decides the limit between the tool and the person?
A named person, not a technical setting. The limit is a service decision: which requests the assistant handles alone, which it passes on, and on which signals.
It has an owner, it is written down, and it is reviewed.
Without an owner, the limit moves on its own, update after update, without anyone having chosen it.
How do you know the limit is in the right place?
By listening to two sources:
customers, through their feedback and repeated requests, and
advisers, who see what reaches them after the handover.
If advisers often receive misunderstood requests, the tool keeps control too long.
If they receive simple requests, it hands over too early.
The percentage of requests handled alone is a result to read with care: it matters less than the satisfaction of those who went through the tool.
Where do you start in your customer service?
With the most frequent and simplest requests: that is where automation frees up the most time, with the least risk.
At the same time, define from day one the signals that trigger a handover to a person. Then check that this handover is visible and quick.
Then widen gradually, always keeping the same rule:
the tool handles the volume,
the person handles what matters.
Which question should you ask your teams?
Just one: in which cases did your customer feel they were talking to someone who did not understand them?
The answers almost always draw the boundary the company has not drawn yet.
That is where the quality of the relationship is decided, far more than in the percentage of requests handled.
What should be passed on to the person taking over?
The full context: the initial request, the answers already given, the information the customer has already provided and the exact point where the exchange stalled.
The person should be able to reply without asking a single question already asked.
This summary is prepared in advance, with the teams who receive the requests, and tested regularly on real cases.
How do you involve frontline teams?
By giving them a voice on the boundary. Advisers know which requests recur, which get complicated and which are better handled in person. Their view avoids moving the limit blindly.
A regular review of a few real exchanges, with them, is enough to spot useful adjustments.
Which indicator should you follow first?
Less the share of requests handled alone than the satisfaction of those who went through the tool, and the time it takes to reach a person when they want one.
A high automation rate can hide real frustration.
The right goal is not to make human exchanges disappear but to reserve them for the moments where they matter most.
How do you test the set-up before rolling it out?
By replaying real requests, including the most delicate: a complaint, an emergency, a badly worded question. Observe at what point the tool should have handed over, and what the person receives at that moment.
A test of a few dozen exchanges, reviewed by advisers, teaches more than a successful demonstration on three carefully chosen cases.
What should you tell the customer so they trust the tool?
The truth: they are talking to an assistant, here is what it can do, and here is how to reach a person.
A customer who has been told accepts the tool’s limits better than one who finds out, mid-conversation, that they are not talking to a human.
Transparency is also a courtesy: it shows the company stands behind what it has put in place.
How do you prepare advisers to take over?
By teaching them to pick up without repeating questions already asked, and to recognise the tone of an already weary customer. Taking over a conversation is a professional skill in its own right, worth a short training.
Advisers must also know when to tell the team that a reason for handover keeps coming back, so the boundary can be adjusted.
How do you keep control as the tool evolves?
By treating each change as a boundary to decide, not as a technical update. Before widening the assistant’s scope, the question is simple: which new requests will the assistant handle alone, and who checks that this stays acceptable for the customer?
A regular review of a few real exchanges, at each change, protects the quality of the relationship.
💬 In your customer service,
where do you draw this limit?
Sources: Usine Digitale, L’Écho touristique (2024-2025); Salesforce, 7th "State of Service" report, survey of 6,500 service professionals (Salesforce News, November 2025).
#ArtificialIntelligence #CustomerRelations #CustomerExperience #CustomerService #EXECIA
Read the full articleabout 3,000 words→
Does an SME need a conversational assistant?
Not always. Before installing anything, I ask one question: how many identical requests does your team receive each week?
If they number in the dozens, a good FAQ page, an automatic email reply and a booking link often cover the essentials, for far less money. An assistant becomes useful when those repetitive requests genuinely eat into the team’s time.
How much does a badly set-up assistant cost?
More than you think, because the cost shows up on no invoice. Clients who give up without saying a word, advisers rescuing conversations that started badly, a brand image that suffers in online reviews.
You have to go looking for these costs: read a few real conversations regularly, track client reviews, ask your advisers. One hour a month is often enough to avoid months of silent decline.
How do you choose a vendor?
Beyond the demo, I look at six criteria:
does the tool answer only from sources you control?
does the handover to a person pass on the full context?
does the tool connect to your software, especially your customer relationship tool?
where is the data hosted, and how long is it kept?
can you easily review the conversation history?
can someone without technical skills update the information?
A vague answer on any of these points weighs more than a spectacular feature.
The quality of answers depends on what you give it
An assistant only knows what it has been taught. If your prices, lead times or conditions change and nobody updates its knowledge base, it answers with total confidence… using outdated information.
So you need a content owner, separate from the technical owner. Their job: keep what the tool uses up to date, and check with every rule change that the assistant takes it into account.
What should happen when the tool does not know?
It should say so. A well-configured assistant answers only from sources the company has validated. When a question falls outside that scope, it admits it.
An invented answer, even a plausible one, costs more than “I do not know, let me put you in touch with someone”. This instruction is written down in black and white during set-up, and tested with trick questions.
What the AI Act changes for assistants
From 2 August 2026, the European AI regulation imposes a transparency obligation: anyone interacting with an AI system must be told so, unless it is obvious from the context.
For a company, getting compliant is simple: a clear message at the start of the exchange, telling the client they are talking to an assistant and how to reach a person. It is also what builds trust.
Personal data in conversations
Clients often share more than you would imagine: a file number, an address, sometimes health or family details. These exchanges fall under the GDPR.
Three precautions:
keep conversations only as long as needed, with a retention period set in advance;
check where the vendor hosts the data and what it does with it;
never ask the client for more than their request requires.
One service across every channel
Website, email, WhatsApp, phone: clients move from one to another without thinking. If they get a different answer depending on the channel, they stop believing any of them.
The same information, the same rules for handing over to a person and the same tone must apply everywhere. To me, that is the real lesson from Air France: one single assistant, rather than a collection of tools that contradict each other.
Nights and weekends?
An assistant answers at any hour. Your teams do not. No need to hide it: organise what comes next.
When nobody is available, the tool can collect the request, sum up the key points and announce a realistic callback time. A client who knows they will be called back tomorrow at ten waits calmly. One going round in circles in a dead-end conversation does not.
The advisers’ job changes
This is an effect people often forget. When the assistant handles the simple requests, advisers only get the difficult cases: complaints, emergencies, clients who are already annoyed.
Their day becomes more demanding, emotionally and intellectually. Plan for it: training for tense situations, recovery time between two difficult exchanges, recognition of this new expertise. Otherwise, automation moves the fatigue around instead of reducing it.
Two more indicators to watch
Beyond satisfaction, two measures flag a problem quickly:
the recontact rate, meaning the share of clients who come back with the same request in the following days;
satisfaction measured right after a handover to a person.
A rising recontact rate means incomplete answers. Low satisfaction after a handover means a poorly prepared transfer. Both can be fixed, as long as you look at them.
Public complaints on social media?
They deserve a rule of their own. An unhappy public message is read by hundreds of people. One clumsy automatic reply, and you have a controversy.
My rule: a first human reply, short and personal, offering to continue in private. AI can help spot these messages and prepare a draft. But the public reply carries the company’s signature: it goes through a person, every time.
Requests in several languages?
Current tools understand and reply in many languages. You can serve foreign clients without hiring.
Stay careful on binding topics, though: one nuance mistranslated in a refund condition, and you have a dispute. In those cases, hand over to a person who masters the language.
Should the assistant have a first name?
Air France called its assistant Louis. A first name makes the exchange warmer and gives the service an identity. But it must not make the client believe they are talking to a person.
The right balance fits in one welcome sentence: a first name, a clear statement that it is an assistant, and a way to reach someone. Warmth does not rule out transparency. It makes it easier to accept.
A typical example
Take a service SME that gets around a hundred questions a week about its opening hours, lead times and file tracking. It hands these three topics to an assistant, fed by a knowledge base that a designated person keeps up to date.
Everything else, complaints, quotes, special cases, goes to the team with a summary of the exchange. After three months, the team has won back several hours a week, the recontact rate is stable, and clients know from the very first message that they can reach a person.
What the Air France example really teaches
You recognise a successful assistant by the moment it steps aside. Answering part of the requests alone is useful. Recognising the moment when a person must take over is what makes the difference.
It is a service decision as much as a technical setting. It belongs to leadership, because it shapes the relationship with every one of your clients.
Valérie Mailland
Founder of EXEC'IA Consulting. 20+ years alongside executives, including 18 in executive coordination at McKinsey & Company. Follow me on LinkedIn →

## An AI recorder in the management meeting: who decided that?
URL : https://exec-ia.ai/perspective-enregistreur-ia-reunion-direction-en.html

← All articles Blog • Governance
An AI recorder in the management meeting: who decided that?
Updated on October 15, 2026
Short version →
SME leaders: AI recorders are entering management meetings, often with no rules, because they save precious time.
The company’s most confidential words then leave for a tool nobody has approved, run by a vendor that may use them.
Four rules are enough to keep the benefit: inform, obtain consent, protect the data, decide who keeps what.
You run an SME and someone has already put a small device on the management table, or let an AI assistant join the video call?
The minutes arrive within the hour, and that is valuable.
One question remains that nobody has asked: who decided this, and where do these conversations go?
🎯 What does an AI recorder do?
The recorder records the meeting, transcribes it, then draws out a summary, the decisions and the list of actions. It comes as a small device on the table, or as an assistant that joins video calls automatically.
The gain is real: nobody takes notes, everyone listens, and the minutes can go out the same day.
What the lawsuit against Otter.ai alleges
In August 2025, a class action was filed in California against Otter.ai, one of the most widely used meeting assistants. The complaint says its assistant recorded participants without their consent, and that the recordings were used to train the vendor’s models.
According to the complaint, only the meeting host gave consent. Other participants were not always told. In August 2026, a California court let several of these claims go forward without ruling on the merits: nobody has been found liable at this stage. Other assistants, such as Granola, are now targeted too.
The real risk in a management meeting
A management meeting talks about acquisitions, salaries, struggling clients, departures. Recording these exchanges with a consumer tool means handing them to a third party without a suitable contract. That is shadow AI, at the very heart of leadership.
🎯 Four rules before recording:
inform every participant, at the start of every meeting;
obtain their consent, and offer traditional note-taking to anyone who declines;
protect the data with a business-grade tool that does not train its models on your conversations;
decide who keeps the recording and the summary, and for how long.
I use an AI recorder myself for my working notes. The benefit is such that it would be a pity to go without. On one condition: that leadership sets the rules before the habit takes hold.
💬 In your management team,
who decided to record?
Sources: NPR, “Class-action suit claims Otter AI secretly records private work conversations”, 15 August 2025; Mondaq, “When AI takes notes, court allows privacy claims against Otter.ai to proceed”, 25 August 2026; French Labour Code, Article L1222-4; CNIL, the GDPR (in French); Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Articles 5 and 50.
#EXECIA #ArtificialIntelligence #ManagementTeam #SMEs #Governance
Read the full articleabout 2,450 words→
Why these tools are appealing
A management meeting produces decisions, and every decision calls for actions. For years someone took notes by hand, then spent an evening writing the minutes. The recorder does that work in a few minutes.
It also frees attention. Someone who no longer takes notes listens, follows up, challenges. For a small management team, where everyone wears several hats, the gain is counted in hours every week.
What changes when everything is recorded
A management meeting is also a place to think out loud. You test a fragile idea, voice a doubt about a client, soften a judgement about a colleague. When everyone knows it is all being recorded, these words become rarer.
The real discussions may then drift to the corridor or the phone, away from any trace. Recording was meant to keep the memory of decisions; it can end up pushing decisions out of the meeting.
Where the recordings go
Before adopting a tool, five answers must appear in its contract:
in which country the recordings are stored;
which subcontractors have access;
whether the vendor uses them to train its models;
how long it keeps them;
how to delete them for good.
Free or consumer plans rarely answer these five questions well. Business plans do so more often, provided you read the contract and not just the presentation page.
Video calls are a case apart
In a video call, the recording assistant often joins the meeting on its own, because a participant linked it to their calendar. It appears as one more guest, with a discreet name that nobody notices.
The organiser remains responsible for what happens in their meeting. They can refuse entry to an unknown assistant, and point to the tool the company has approved. A setting made once in the video tool avoids many surprises.
What French law says
A recorded business meeting contains personal data: participants’ voices, words and opinions. The GDPR applies: a precise purpose, clear information, a limited retention period, rights of access and erasure.
The Labour Code adds a simple rule, in Article L1222-4: no information concerning an employee personally may be collected by a device that has not been brought to their attention beforehand. If the tool can be used to monitor employees’ activity, the works council must also be informed and consulted, in companies that have one.
What the AI Act says
Some tools offer to analyse participants’ tone, mood or engagement. In the workplace, emotion recognition by AI has been banned since 2 February 2025, except for medical or safety reasons. It is better to turn these functions off, or to choose a tool that does not offer them.
The transparency rule in force since 2 August 2026 applies too: everyone must know when a piece of content, such as a meeting summary, is produced by an AI.
Meetings never to record
Some meetings have no place in a recorder, whatever the tool:
one-to-one interviews with an employee;
discussions about acquisitions, disposals or fundraising;
exchanges with a lawyer, protected by professional privilege;
health or personal-situation topics;
pay decisions.
For these meetings, traditional note-taking, reviewed by the participants, remains the right method.
What the lawsuit against Otter.ai teaches
Filed in August 2025 before a federal court in California, the complaint makes three charges against the vendor. Its assistant allegedly recorded participants who had not given consent. Only the meeting host was allegedly asked. Default settings allegedly turned off warnings before the meeting.
The vendor replies that recordings are “de-identified” before they are used to improve its speech recognition. These are allegations. In August 2026, a California court let several claims go forward, which is not a finding of liability: the merits have not been judged. The lesson can still be read without waiting for a verdict: a tool’s default settings are not those of a company mindful of its obligations. Check them one by one.
Three ways to proceed
From the most cautious to the most open, three positions are defensible:
no recording: one person takes the notes, reviewed by the participants;
occasional recording: for a specific meeting, with everyone’s consent and deletion of the audio after the summary;
regular recording of operational meetings, governed by the policy, excluding sensitive topics.
For an SME management team, I recommend the second position for three months. It lets you judge the real gain before a habit settles in.
The case of personal recorders
In many SMEs the recorder arrives through an employee: a device bought privately, put on the table “to save time”. The company has not approved it, knows neither its host nor its terms, and does not know where the recordings go.
The right reaction is not a sanction. It is better to offer a simple conversation: acknowledge the need, show the approved tool that covers it, agree a date after which only that one is used. An employee with nothing to fear reports their own tools.
Where a recorder really helps
The tool is most useful in project follow-up meetings and steering committees, where each point leads to an action with an owner and a date. It suits deeper discussions less, where speech holds back as soon as a microphone is on.
A good test: if the minutes are used to chase actions, recording is justified. If they are meant to keep a trace of a fragile line of thought, a free exchange followed by a few lines written by a human is better.
The questions your employees will ask
It is better to prepare the answers before they are asked:
who can listen to the recording, and who can only read the summary?
how long is the audio kept, and where?
can I ask for a passage about me to be deleted?
are these recordings used to assess my work?
The last question matters most. The answer must be written in the policy, and it must be no. A recorder used to assess employees changes nature, and it also changes the climate of meetings.
A one-page recording policy
One page is enough to set the management team’s rules:
the approved tool, and only that one;
the meetings covered, and those excluded;
the announcement sentence at the start of a meeting;
who validates the summary, and within what time;
the retention period for the audio, the text and the summary.
This policy ties in with the one that governs the use of AI across the whole company. The management team thus sets the example it asks of the teams.
Announcing the recording
The announcement takes ten seconds. For example: “This meeting is being recorded for the minutes, with our approved tool. The audio will be deleted once the summary is validated. If anyone prefers us to stop, at any point, they only need to say so.”
The last sentence matters most. It allows the recording to be switched off for a sensitive point, with no need to justify it.
Choosing the tool
Five criteria help sort the offers:
a contract that excludes training models on your recordings;
hosting in Europe, or equivalent guarantees;
deletion of the audio once the text is obtained;
named access, reserved for committee members;
a simple export, so as not to depend on the vendor.
The best tool is not the one that writes the finest summaries. It is the one whose workings you can explain to an anxious participant.
The role of the executive assistant
The tool produces a summary. It does not know what was really decided, or what must not circulate. That sorting falls to a person: often the executive assistant, who knows the files and the sensitivities of the committee.
They review the summary, correct errors, remove anything confidential, then have it validated by the chair. The official minutes thus remain a human document, written with the help of a machine.
After the meeting
The validated minutes become the only reference record. The audio no longer has a reason to be kept: deleting it limits the risk in case of a leak or an access request.
A simple check each quarter confirms the rules hold: which recordings still exist, who has access, and whether another tool has slipped into meetings.
What leadership gains
Clear rules do not slow use: they make it possible. Committee members accept recording more readily when they know what will become of it.
Leadership also gains a reliable memory of its decisions, validated and dated. If there is a disagreement six months later about what was decided, the minutes settle it.
A typical meeting, from invitation to summary
A recorded meeting follows three stages:
before: the invitation announces the recording, names the tool and offers an alternative;
during: the chair says the opening sentence, checks the indicator light and stops the recording for sensitive points;
after: the summary is reviewed, validated and filed where agreed, then the audio is deleted.
Each stage has an owner named in the policy, and it is not always the same person.
Mistakes to avoid
Five mistakes come up again and again:
letting everyone choose their own personal tool;
recording every meeting by default;
circulating the summary without review;
keeping the audio indefinitely;
forgetting outside participants, clients or partners.
The last one often comes as a surprise. A partner who discovers afterwards that they were recorded rightly wonders how far they can trust you.
Three signs you need rules
If one of these signs appears, it is time to write the policy:
several recording tools circulate in meetings;
nobody knows where the recordings are stored;
a participant has already asked, during a meeting, whether it was being recorded.
Clients, partners, candidates
Outside participants are not bound by your policy. They discover the recorder when the meeting begins, sometimes from a video waiting room. Tell them in the invitation, with a clear sentence and the option to decline.
Recruitment interviews call for particular care. The European AI regulation lists among high-risk uses the systems used to assess candidates. A recorder that scores or ranks a candidate’s speech goes beyond simple minutes. For these interviews, traditional note-taking remains the rule.
Two sentences to keep handy
To open: “We are recording this meeting with our approved tool, only for the minutes. The audio will be deleted after the summary is validated.”
With a reluctant participant: “Of course, we will stop recording. One person will take notes by hand, and you will review them.” The second sentence matters more than the first: it shows that declining penalises nobody.
What an AI summary can distort
A fluent summary is not an accurate summary. Before validation, five points need checking:
names, especially those that sound alike or come from another country;
figures and dates, which tools sometimes get wrong;
who actually made each decision;
the deadline and the owner of each action;
nuances, irony and conditions: “yes, if…” too often becomes “yes”.
This review takes ten minutes. It protects the company from the false certainty of a well-written text.
Asking the teams what they think
A month after the start, a fifteen-minute conversation with three participants teaches more than a survey. Three questions are enough: has the recording changed what you dare to say? Does the summary reflect the meeting? Did you know where it was filed?
The answers show whether the policy works or stays on paper. They also reveal, quietly, whether the committee speaks differently since it has been recorded: that is the sign to watch first.
Measuring whether it works
Four indicators are enough to judge after three months: the time spent writing minutes, the delay between the meeting and its distribution, the share of actions completed on time, and the number of refusals or reservations expressed. If the time drops and refusals stay rare, the method holds. If not, review the policy before extending.
Security: sharing, access, links
Many tools create a sharing link for each recording by default. A link sent by mistake gives access to the whole meeting. Turn off link sharing, limit access to participants, and enable two-factor authentication on the accounts that hold these recordings.
Check exports too. Summaries copied into a messaging app or a shared document escape the tool’s retention rules. The policy must say where the validated summary is filed, and that it exists nowhere else.
If a recording circulates by mistake
A leak is handled within hours, in this order:
cut access to the link or file concerned;
inform the managing director and the person in charge of data protection;
list who could have listened or read, and what information the meeting contained;
assess whether the CNIL must be informed, within 72 hours when a risk to individuals is established;
inform the participants concerned and fix the setting that caused the error.
Preparing this list in advance avoids improvisation on the day it is needed. It fits on half a page, attached to the policy.
My advice to a business leader
A five-step approach, in one month:
list the tools already used in meetings, without looking for culprits;
choose a single one, after reading the contract;
write the one-page policy with the management team;
give the review of summaries to a designated person;
take stock after three months.
An AI recorder can keep the memory of a meeting. Deciding what deserves to be kept remains the work of leadership.
Valérie Mailland
Founder of EXEC'IA Consulting. 20+ years alongside executives, including 18 in executive coordination at McKinsey & Company. Follow me on LinkedIn →

## Blog: adopting AI is not creating value
URL : https://exec-ia.ai/perspective-entreprise-utilise-deja-ia-en.html

← All articles ★Blog • Governance
Adopting AI is one thing.
Creating value from it
is another.
Article developed from my LinkedIn post (8 September 2026)
Updated on 30 September 2026
Short version →
SME leaders: adopting AI is one thing; creating value from it is another.
80% of companies see their teams save time with AI. Only 37% see the effect on their results.
To pick the uses that deserve real investment, three questions are enough: does it come up often?
Can it be measured?
Does it hold without one expert?
Klarna had to rehire humans after handing its customer service to AI. It had mistaken a time saving for a result.
The question to ask yourself: of all your AI uses, which one deserves to be rolled out across the whole company?
You run an SME and your teams already use AI?
This figure from the latest State of AI report by McKinsey & Company is for you. Across nearly 1,700 organisations in 97 countries, 80% see their teams save time thanks to AI. Yet only 37% see the effect on their operating results.
Everything that remains to be done sits between those two figures.
What strikes me is that AI enters the company through employees, not through leadership. Everyone finds their own shortcut. Summarising meeting notes. Roughing out a first draft. Searching faster. These gains are real, and nobody disputes them. But they stay scattered, and none of them reaches the bottom line on its own.
What if the next challenge for AI were no longer just adoption, but choosing between its uses?
Which uses deserve investment?
Which ones should come first?
And which should you have the discipline to drop?
🎯 Why does the ability to choose become strategic as technological possibilities multiply?
Today, with AI, you can try everything. That is exactly the trap: when you test everything, nobody decides anything.
To choose, I suggest three questions.
1) Does the use come up often?
A tool used every week by several teams weighs more than a spectacular demo done once.
2) Can it be measured?
If nobody can say, six months from now, what it changed, it was never tied to a figure leadership tracks.
3) Does it hold without an expert?
A use that only works thanks to one person will stop the day that person changes jobs.
These three questions come before you invest.
Once the money is spent, saying no becomes much harder.
What does this look like in practice?
Picture a sales team using AI to prepare its prospects before the first call.
They use it every day. The result can be measured: the conversion rate of that first meeting. The tool keeps running even if the person who set it up leaves.
Three questions, three yeses.
Now picture an internal chatbot launched to “show the company is ahead of the curve”. Hardly anyone uses it, and no figure is tracked.
Three questions, three nos.
Want an even quicker test?
Ask yourself whether anyone would notice it in a figure leadership already looks at, if this use vanished tomorrow.
How do you put this trade-off in place without adding a new layer?
In an SME, you do not need a committee or a new job for this. One person is enough, often someone already on the team. You give them a clear mission: run every AI project through the three questions before any money goes in.
They do not need to be technical. They need to know both sides:
• the people on the ground who use the tools, and
• the figures leadership follows.
It is often the role a leader’s right hand already plays, without the title.
One question to see where you stand:
at your company, who can say no to an AI tool that fails the three questions, even if the team loves it?
If no name comes to mind, your uses are settling in on their own. Nobody chose them.
What does this change for a mid-sized company’s AI budget?
It changes how you split the budget. Before buying a new tool, keep a small share of the AI budget to check the ones already running. One question is enough: how many are tracked by a figure leadership looks at every month?
That check costs little, a few hours as a rule. It often stops you from putting more money into a tool that never went beyond one person’s comfort.
It has another benefit. It brings out the uses that, on the contrary, deserve a push: the ones nobody thought of raising with leadership.
That is the question I want to dig into with you: how do you get from everything AI makes possible to the decisions that create value?
How do you tell an individual gain from an outcome?
I sort things into two columns. On one side, what makes a task lighter. On the other, what changes a result.
Meeting notes summarised faster?
That is a gain for one person.
A decision made sooner, a client better prepared before the first call, an error caught before it costs money?
Now we are talking about results.
The first gain shows up straight away, but nobody remembers it three months later.
The second has to be sought out, measured and chosen from the start. It never happens by chance.
The same McKinsey report shows an interesting shift. The share of large companies deploying AI agents across the whole organisation, and no longer in a single department, rose from 27% to 40% in one year.
To me, these are the companies starting to move beyond individual gains. They chose where to put their effort, instead of letting every team test things in its own corner.
For an executive committee, the question becomes: “which use, once chosen and backed, will change a figure we already track?”
It comes before choosing the tool.
In real life, nobody is well placed to decide alone. The employee who found the clever shortcut has neither the overview nor the authority to extend it.
Leadership has the authority. But it rarely has the time to test everything coming up from the field.
In between, someone is often missing. Someone who knows the field well enough to spot what is worth it, and knows leadership well enough to tie it to a figure it tracks.
Who should own this trade-off?
Someone whose mission it clearly is. In most companies, the tools are there. So is the goodwill. What is missing is a person in charge of deciding between what comes up from the field and leadership’s priorities.
In a large company, that may be a head of transformation. In an SME, it is often the leader, their right hand or the finance director. The title does not matter. What matters is that everyone knows who decides, and that this person is allowed to say no.
Without that name, every team keeps its own tools, subscriptions pile up, and nobody knows which ones are worth anything.
Where should you start?
With an inventory. List the AI uses already in place at your company: there are almost always more than you think.
Then run each one through the three questions.
Most leadership teams then discover they are already paying, without knowing it, for tools that pass none of the tests, while one or two others deserve backing.
The inventory often fits into one meeting. The hard part comes after: agreeing to stop a tool everyone got used to, because it fails the test, even if nobody has complained yet.
What does a real case reveal about confusing individual gain with outcome?
The story of Klarna, the Swedish buy-now-pay-later company, says a lot. In February 2024, its chief executive announced that its AI assistant was doing the work of 700 full-time customer service agents, and answering faster.
A year later, the company was rehiring human agents. It explained publicly that with AI alone, it could not keep service quality up.
The first figure measured a gain: fewer calls, faster answers. It said nothing about what the company tracks day to day: how satisfied and loyal its customers stay over time.
That is the whole point. A gain that shows up straight away only becomes a result once it has been checked against the figure leadership already tracks.
💬 And in your organisation,
is the challenge still adopting AI…
or now knowing where it deserves to be deployed?
Source: McKinsey & Company, “The State of AI in 2026: On the road to ROI”, August 2026.
#ArtificialIntelligence #AIStrategy #Transformation #Leadership #ValueCreation
Going further
Four more questions to take the thinking further.
Read the full articleabout 3,000 words→
Three families of uses, three levels of value
Not all AI uses are equal. Lump them together and you end up comparing things that cannot be compared.
I sort them into three families:
comfort uses, which lighten one person’s workload: writing, summarising, translating;
process uses, which change the way several people work together: handling requests, preparing quotes, chasing follow-ups;
decision uses, which change what leadership knows at the moment of choosing: analysing margins, spotting at-risk customers, forecasting workload.
The first family spreads on its own. The other two only move forward if someone carries them, because they touch the organisation itself.
How do you put a value on a use, simply?
A back-of-the-envelope calculation is enough to start: the time saved each time, multiplied by the number of times in the month, multiplied by the hourly cost of the people involved.
Against that, put everything the use costs. The subscription, of course, but not only.
Four costs often slip through the cracks:
review time, essential as long as the tool can get things wrong;
training time, at the start and then with every new hire;
upkeep of the instructions given to the tool, which age along with your products and your rules;
coordination time, when the use moves from one team to another.
A tool that saves you ten minutes but needs eight to check saves you nothing. It just moves the work around.
How do you avoid the pilot that never ends?
Many companies pile up trials that never turn into decisions. The test drags on, the team gets used to it, and nobody decides.
The fix fits in one rule: set the exit before the entry. Before launching a trial, write down how long it lasts, the figure you will track and the threshold at which you roll it out or stop.
A pilot with no end date is no longer a pilot. It is a use installed by default, one nobody will ever have to evaluate.
What role for the finance function?
A central one, and often forgotten. Finance knows the real costs, can read a gain, and already runs the meetings where spending is decided.
Bring them in early. The conversation changes: you stop talking about a tool people like, and start talking about the return on an investment, with the same standards as any other project.
In an SME without a finance director, the accountant or the leader can play that role. On one condition: looking at AI uses with the same rigour as every other expense.
Why does data quality so often decide the result?
An AI tool is only as good as what you give it. An incomplete customer file, prices scattered across several documents, procedures nobody ever wrote down: even the most powerful tool will not get much out of that.
Before looking for the best tool, ask yourself a simple question: does the information this use needs exist, is it up to date, and is someone responsible for it?
If the answer is no, your first project is putting that information in order. AI will come after.
How do you present a decision to the executive committee?
On a single page, with five headings:
the use, described in one sentence everyone understands;
the figure tracked, with its value before and after;
the full cost, subscription included;
the main risk, and how to keep it under control;
the proposed decision: roll out, adjust or stop.
This format forces clarity. If a use does not fit on one page, it is not ready to be decided yet.
When should you speed up rather than slow down?
Choosing does not mean slowing down. When a use passes the three questions, the right decision is often to move fast, before the momentum fades.
To roll out a use, four steps:
document it, with the instructions that work and the mistakes to avoid;
train new teams on their own cases, not on a generic demo;
equip it, with a business plan suited to the number of users;
measure again three months later, to check the gain holds at a larger scale.
A use that works in one team is good news. It becomes a result for the company the day it works elsewhere, without the person who found it.
Do you need a separate AI budget?
Not necessarily. A separate budget attracts projects looking for money more than projects answering a need.
I prefer another route: each function pays for its uses out of its own budget, with one shared rule. Every expense is tied to a figure the function already tracks. AI then becomes one way among others to reach an existing goal, rather than an expense to justify for its own sake.
A small central reserve can complete the picture, to fund the uses that cut across several teams and belong to nobody.
What about ideas that fit into no box?
Keep a small space for them, limited in time and in resources. Some ideas do not pass the three questions yet simply because they are too new to be measured.
Give them a small share of the effort, with a clear deadline. You do not stifle innovation, and you do not let it take over your priorities. At the deadline, the idea joins the normal decision process, or it stops.
And what about the competition?
The fear of falling behind often pushes companies to multiply trials. I understand that fear. But it is looking at the wrong risk.
Falling behind does not come from the number of tools tested. It comes from being unable to turn good trials into shared practices. A company that tests little but rolls out well moves faster than one that tests everything and decides nothing.
How do you know the process is working?
Three signs to look for after six months:
fewer uses running, but more of them tracked by a figure;
at least one use stopped, and explained to the teams;
at least one use extended beyond the team that found it.
If no use has been stopped, the choosing probably never happened. It was only announced.
What choosing really changes
Choosing means accepting to give things up. Attractive uses, flattering demos, sometimes even the tool the leader likes.
In return, the company gains something rare: the ability to focus its attention on what changes its results. When possibilities multiply every month, that is an advantage in its own right.
How do you link an AI use to a company result?
→
Follow the thread from the task to the decision. Which task does the tool shorten?
How much time does it free up?
What is that time used for next?
The last question is the one that counts. Without it, the gain stays individual.
A simple test: try saying out loud “thanks to this use, we decide or deliver faster what matters to our customers”. If the sentence does not ring true, the use is not yet linked to a result.
An example. A tool drafts meeting notes and saves a manager one hour a week. If that hour goes into calling back two waiting clients, the gain becomes a result. If it disappears into emails, nobody will ever see it.
Which indicator should you choose to judge a first use?
→
Just one, and one everybody understands: the time saved on a precise task, the number of errors avoided, or the response time to a customer. Track five, and nobody looks at any of them.
Choose it before the test, never after. Otherwise you always end up picking the figure that confirms what you hoped.
Write down the starting point too. Without a figure before the trial, you cannot prove progress afterwards.
One week of very simple tracking, even by hand, is enough for that baseline.
It is the step most often forgotten, and it is what makes the decision indisputable in committee.
How often should you review your choices?
→
Often, and without making a big deal of it. Once a quarter is a good rhythm. Tools change fast, so do uses, and a decision made a year ago may no longer match what is happening today.
No need for a long committee. A list of uses, what each one brought, and a decision for each: keep, adjust or stop.
The simplest way: hook this review onto a meeting that already exists, such as the quarterly budget review. It then no longer depends on anyone’s goodwill, and it does not get dropped when the diary fills up.
What do you tell teams when a use is stopped?
→
The truth, simply.
A team that understands why a tool is being stopped accepts the decision more easily. It will even suggest another solution more readily.
Stopping a use is part of the job. It even proves the company is choosing, instead of piling up tools.
Remember to thank those who tested it. Their trial taught you something, even if the answer is no. A team that is not penalised for a stopped test will want to try another. That is how a culture of trying takes root, without anyone being afraid of getting it wrong.
Valérie Mailland
Founder of EXEC'IA Consulting. 20+ years alongside executives, including 18 in executive coordination at McKinsey & Company. Follow me on LinkedIn →
