## AI giants move in with clients. And your SME?
URL : https://exec-ia.ai/perspective-forward-deployed-engineer-pme-en.html

← All articles Blog • Deployment
AI giants now move in with their clients.
What about your SME?
Updated on October 15, 2026
Short version →
SME leaders: Amazon has just put $1 billion into engineers who work on site with its clients, so that AI actually delivers.
This job, the “forward deployed engineer”, shows where the value lies: in translating between leadership, the tool and the real work of teams.
An SME does not need a full-time engineer. It needs a translator between AI and the business, and someone to stay until the new habit sticks.
You run an SME and you have tried AI, yet it has not really changed the way your teams work?
The largest tech companies hit the same wall.
They created a new job to break through it. Here is what an SME can learn from it, without hiring an engineer.
🎯 What is a “forward deployed engineer”?
An engineer sent to work at the client’s site, sometimes for months, to make AI work in day-to-day reality. They watch how people work, connect the tool to the company’s data, adjust it, and stay until the teams actually use it.
The role was born at Palantir in the early 2010s. It is now one of the most sought-after jobs in tech.
What Amazon did
On 30 June 2026, AWS, Amazon’s cloud arm, announced $1 billion to build a whole organisation of these engineers, embedded with clients in small teams. Its stated goal: to leave behind systems that run and skills that stay in-house.
Amazon is not alone: according to HR Executive, AWS joins OpenAI and Anthropic in this race. According to Indeed, job postings for this role rose by more than 729% in a year, from April 2025 to April 2026.
Why this job is booming
According to an MIT report published in August 2025, 95% of corporate generative AI pilots had no measurable impact on results. The technology works. What is missing is someone to bring it into real work.
What this job reveals
The problem is not the tool. It is the translation between what leadership wants, what the tool can do and what teams actually do on a Monday morning.
An SME has no forward deployed engineer, and no budget to pay for one. Yet it has the same need: someone to translate.
🎯 The three roles of the translator, which an SME can fill without hiring:
understand the business before talking about tools;
turn a leadership decision into a concrete use, on one specific task;
stay until the use sticks, then hand over.
For more than twenty years alongside executives, my job was to turn their decisions into concrete action for their teams. With AI, that translator is exactly what most SMEs lack.
💬 In your company,
who translates between AI and leadership?
Sources: SiliconANGLE, “AWS launches forward-deployed engineering team”, 30 June 2026; LeadDev, citing Indeed data shared with Business Insider, April 2026; Fortune, MIT report on generative AI pilots, 18 August 2025; HR Executive, “AWS joins OpenAI and Anthropic in race to embed engineers inside enterprises”, 22 July 2026; Wikipedia, “Forward Deployed Engineer”; Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 50; GDPR.
#EXECIA #ArtificialIntelligence #SMEs #Deployment #Governance
Read the full articleabout 2,300 words→
Where the job comes from
In the early 2010s, Palantir sold data analysis software to government agencies and large corporations. The products were powerful, but no client could plug them alone into scattered, messy, tightly protected data. So the company sent its engineers on site.
These engineers sold nothing and wrote no reports. They sat next to the users, learned their work and adapted the software until it was useful. For years the model looked expensive and reserved for a few prestigious clients. Generative AI has put it back at the centre.
Why the giants are doing it now
AI models look more and more alike, and their prices keep falling. The difference lies in how they connect to the data, rules and habits of one specific company. That work cannot be automated: it needs someone in the room.
For a software vendor, a forward deployed engineer is costly. The return comes in another form: a client who truly uses the tool and stops shopping around. AI giants are willing to trim their margins to win that loyalty.
A day in the life
The work almost always follows the same thread:
watch a team at work, before proposing anything;
find the useful data and the people who hold the keys;
build a first prototype in a few days, on a real task;
put it into service within the client’s security rules;
train the users, then measure what has changed.
The prototype matters less than the first two steps. A tool built without watching the work answers a question nobody is asking.
Why talk about a translator
Here, translating does not mean changing language. The translator turns a leadership decision into a precise task, the vocabulary of the business into that of the tool, and the machine’s answer into a sentence the teams understand.
A good translator also knows how to say what cannot be translated. “This tool cannot do that” is a precious sentence: it saves months of disappointed waiting.
What the engineer does not do
They do not set the company’s priorities. They do not replace managers in leading the change. They do not decide which task deserves to be handed to a machine. Those choices belong to leadership.
When leadership does not make them, even the most brilliant engineer builds tools that serve no purpose. The whole job rests on a clear decision, made upstream.
The lesson for an SME
The tool gets cheaper every year. Integration still takes as much time and attention as ever. An SME that budgets for licences without planning who will bring them to life repeats the mistake the giants are now fixing with billions.
The good news: in an SME, the path is shorter. Fewer layers, fewer systems, leaders close to the ground. The translator role fits within a handful of people.
A skill rather than a job title
An SME does not create a forward deployed engineer position. It needs the skill: understanding a leadership decision, turning it into a concrete use, following that use over time.
This skill is rarely technical. It relies on knowing the business, earning the teams’ trust and having access to leadership. The people who have it are often already on the payroll.
Who can play this role in your SME
Four profiles come up often:
the managing director or a partner, when the subject is strategic;
the executive assistant, who knows the files and the decision paths;
a curious operations manager, respected by their team;
short-term outside support, to frame the project and then hand over.
The right person is not the one who knows the tool best. It is the one the teams listen to, and the one leadership consults.
The pair that works
Translation rests on two people: one who speaks the language of the business and of leadership, one who speaks the language of the tool. The second can be a contractor, a vendor or an employee at ease with digital tools.
The usual mistake is to hand the project to the technician alone. They deliver a tool that matches the specifications and that nobody uses, because nobody translated the real need.
Questions to ask before you start
Five questions prevent most false starts:
which leadership decision does this project serve?
which specific task must change, and for whom?
where is the data we need, and who has access to it?
how will we know, three months from now, that it works?
who stays with the team after the launch?
If the fifth question has no answer, the project will end the day the contractor leaves.
An example to fix ideas
Imagine, as an illustration, a service SME of forty people that prepares around ten quotes a week. The managing director wants AI to help the sales team. This example is invented: it shows the approach, not a mission carried out.
The person who translates first spends two half-days watching how a quote is prepared. They notice that the time is not lost in writing. It is lost in hunting for old quotes and for the terms negotiated with each client.
So the first use is not “write faster”. It is “find the last comparable quote in thirty seconds”. Without that observation, the company would have bought a writing tool that does not solve its problem.
Three objections you will hear
“It is too expensive.” The translator costs a few days. Unused licences cost money every month, for years, without anyone questioning them.
“My teams will fear being replaced.” The fear fades when leadership says clearly what will not change, and when the teams themselves choose the task to lighten. Nobody feels replaced by a tool they asked for.
“We do not have the time.” It takes half a day a week for three months, no more. The real shortage of time comes from repetitive tasks that a good first automation gives back to the teams.
Three starting conditions
Before launching the project, three conditions must be met:
a written leadership decision, read and accepted by the management team;
one person with at least half a day a week for three months;
access to the useful data, with a contact for security questions.
If one of the three is missing, it is better to postpone by a few weeks. A project launched without them runs out of steam at the first obstacle.
The “45” rule at AWS
According to SiliconANGLE, AWS sets its teams a goal in three numbers: 45 minutes to formulate the idea, 45 hours to validate it, 45 days to deliver it. The aim is speed, with a verifiable result at every stage.
An SME does not have to copy these numbers. It can keep the spirit: frame the task in one meeting, test on a real case within two weeks, go live within forty-five days. Each stage produces proof, which convinces the next team.
Choosing the first use
The first use must succeed quickly to win people over. It meets four criteria:
a task that comes back every week;
data that is already available, without a major project;
a measurable result: time saved, errors avoided;
a team willing to give it a try.
A quote prepared faster, a better-targeted customer follow-up, meeting minutes sent the same day: the best first uses are modest and visible.
Stay until it sticks
The real know-how of a forward deployed engineer is not leaving too early. A new habit is fragile in the weeks after launch: the first glitch, the first disappointing result, the pull of old routines.
In an SME, three check-points are enough:
at 30 days, gather what gets in the way and fix it;
at 60 days, measure actual use and the result achieved;
at 90 days, decide to extend, adjust or stop.
Measuring what has changed
Login counts tell you nothing. The right indicators show up in the work itself: time spent on the task before and after, errors that have disappeared, people who come back to the tool without being asked.
A twenty-minute conversation with three users often teaches more than a dashboard. It also reveals what the tool cannot do yet.
Data and security
Connecting AI to company data calls for a few simple rules. Choose a business plan that contractually excludes using your data to train models. Give named access only. Never put customer data into a consumer tool.
The GDPR applies as soon as personal data is involved. Under the AI Act, the transparency rule in force since 2 August 2026 is easy to meet: everyone must know when they are dealing with an AI.
What the translator costs
A forward deployed engineer at a tech giant means months of full-time work. An SME does not need that volume. A few days spread over three months, well placed, are often enough: at the framing stage, at launch and at each check-point.
The heaviest cost lies elsewhere: in licences paid for a tool nobody uses, and in the distrust a failed project leaves the teams for the next one.
Mistakes to avoid
Five mistakes come up again and again:
buying the tool before choosing the task;
handing the project to the technician alone;
rolling out everywhere at once;
leaving on launch day;
judging success by the number of licences opened.
They all share one root: treating AI as a purchase, when it changes a way of working.
Three signs a translator is missing
These signs do not lie:
AI subscriptions that few employees ever open;
successful pilots that are never extended;
leaders who are convinced, teams who wait and see.
One is enough. It shows the decision exists but has not yet reached the real work.
A week-by-week calendar
Over twelve weeks, the project follows a simple rhythm:
week 1: write the leadership decision and observe the team concerned;
week 2: locate the data and obtain access;
weeks 3 and 4: build a first trial with two volunteers;
weeks 5 and 6: fix what gets in the way, based on their feedback;
weeks 7 and 8: open the tool to the whole team;
weeks 9 and 10: train, and write the rules of use on one page;
weeks 11 and 12: measure, then decide to extend, adjust or stop.
Leaving a shared vocabulary
According to SiliconANGLE, AWS aims to build at its clients what it calls a semantic layer, that is, a company vocabulary that machines understand. The idea carries over very simply to an SME.
Words change meaning from one department to another. An “active client” is not the same for accounting and for sales; neither is a “signed quote”. An AI that reads these words without telling them apart is confidently wrong.
A one-page glossary, written with the teams, fixes much of this. It is often the translator’s most useful deliverable, and the only one that remains after they leave.
Choosing an outside partner
If you call on a provider, five questions help you judge:
did they observe your teams’ work before proposing a tool?
what will they leave behind once the assignment ends?
who owns the documents, settings and access?
what does the contract say about the use of your data?
are they paid on your result, or on selling licences?
The last question often reveals the essentials. A provider who lives off licences has an interest in selling more of them. A partner who lives off your result has an interest in the use taking hold.
The limits of the model
The model has a known flaw: it creates dependence. An outside translator ends up as the only one who knows the tool, the settings and the history of the project. If they leave, the use becomes fragile.
The remedy takes three steps: train an internal relay in the first month, write down what was decided and why, and set in advance the date when the support ends. A good translator prepares their departure from day one.
The model is also wrong if leadership has not yet decided what it expects from AI. In that case, the first job is not to deploy but to help the management team choose. It is often the quickest part, and the most profitable.
What you can prepare this month
Without buying anything, four steps prepare the ground:
list five tasks that come back every week in the team of your choice;
ask two colleagues which one takes the most of their time;
find where the necessary documents are, and who has access;
block in the diary the weekly half-day of the person who will translate.
This preparation takes an hour. It is often enough to show whether the company is ready, or whether the decision needs clarifying first.
My advice to a business leader
A five-step approach, sized for an SME:
write down, in one sentence, the decision AI should serve;
name the person who will translate, and give them time;
choose a modest first use, with a willing team;
follow that use at 30, 60 and 90 days;
extend only what has proved its worth.
This is the role I play at EXEC’IA: translating AI into leadership decisions, then staying alongside until the use takes hold, with technical partners when the project calls for them.
AI giants have understood that value is created at the client’s site. In an SME, it is created between leadership and the teams.
Valérie Mailland
Founder of EXEC'IA Consulting. 20+ years alongside executives, including 18 in executive coordination at McKinsey & Company. Follow me on LinkedIn →

## When a leader leaves, how do you keep their knowledge?
URL : https://exec-ia.ai/perspective-jumeau-numerique-savoir-dirigeant-en.html

← All articles Blog • Succession
When a leader leaves,
how do you keep their knowledge?
Article developed from my LinkedIn post (13/10/2026) · Updated on October 13, 2026
Short version →
SME leaders: within ten years, around 550,000 business owners in France will retire.
Sellers prepare the price, the buyer and the tax. Rarely the knowledge: why that client stays, why that supplier, what has already failed.
An AI assistant built on interviews with the leader can keep that memory, provided the leader approves everything passed on.
You run an SME and your departure is on the horizon, in three years or in ten?
Your knowledge appears in no sale agreement.
This article helps you keep it inside the company, with AI and under your control.
🎯 What is a leader’s digital twin?
An AI assistant that answers questions from what the leader has said, written and decided. It doesn’t replace the leader. It keeps a record of their reasoning for whoever takes over.
The term comes from industry, where engineers build a digital copy of a machine to monitor it remotely. Applied to a leader, it means a memory you can ask questions.
What Frédéric Mazzella did
In July 2026, the founder of BlaBlaCar launched Fred24, an AI assistant built on twenty years of his talks, interviews and writing. Entrepreneurs ask it questions; it answers from what Frédéric Mazzella has already said and written.
His audience is broad: people starting a business. The same idea works inside an SME, for a small circle: the successor, the leadership team, key managers.
The figures that make it urgent
According to the French Ministry of the Economy, around 550,000 business owners will retire within ten years, with 3 million jobs at stake. The “Objectif Reprises” plan, presented on 23 April 2026, aims to make these handovers easier.
Knowledge, the forgotten asset in a sale
The “Great Insights 2026” survey by Great Place To Work and Toluna (4,246 working people) confirms it: 44% of employees can name colleagues whose departure would take important knowledge with them. Only 40% see their company organising that transfer.
A leader concentrates this risk. They know why a client stays loyal, why a supplier was chosen, what has been tried and failed. None of it shows in the accounts.
🎯 A four-step method, while the leader is still there:
record short interviews with them about their key decisions;
have them transcribed and sorted by theme;
give the successor an assistant that answers from these notes and cites its sources;
let the leader review and approve everything passed on.
Two leaders close to me are going through it right now: one retires in three years, the other is selling his company. The timing is right for both: they are still there to tell, correct and pass on.
💬 In your company,
who knows today what your leader knows?
Sources: Bpifrance Big Média, interview with Frédéric Mazzella on Fred24, 15 July 2026 (in French); French Ministry of the Economy, “Objectif Reprises” plan, April 2026 (in French); Great Place To Work and Toluna, “Great Insights 2026” survey (in French); Banque des Territoires, proposed “Papin pact” (in French); Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 50; GDPR.
#EXECIA #ArtificialIntelligence #Succession #SMEs #Governance
Read the full articleabout 1,600 words→
Why a leader’s knowledge gets lost
Many of a leader’s decisions leave no written trace. They happen on the phone, at the end of a meeting, in a corridor. The minutes keep the decision; they almost always lose the reasoning.
The rest lives in their head: the history of a client relationship, the reason behind a price, a commitment made to a partner years ago. When the leader leaves, the successor inherits the contracts without the context that explains them.
What a digital twin can do
Built well, it does three things:
finds, in seconds, information buried in years of notes;
explains the why behind a past decision, with the source to prove it;
says it doesn’t know when a question goes beyond what it was given.
The third matters most. An assistant that invents a plausible answer does more harm than silence.
What it can’t do
It doesn’t decide. It only knows what it was given, as of the day it was given. It replaces neither the handover between two people, nor meetings with key clients, nor the time a successor needs to earn the team’s trust.
Nor does it capture intuition. A leader can explain why they turned a partner down; they can’t pass on the feeling that warned them. The assistant keeps the explanation, not the instinct.
Interviews: the raw material
A few well-prepared one-hour interviews beat a long improvised series. Five themes come up in most SMEs:
long-standing clients, and what keeps them;
suppliers and partners, and why they were chosen;
hard decisions, and what they taught;
past mistakes not to repeat;
the company’s unwritten rules.
The best questions start from a story: “tell me about the last time you turned a client down”. A story carries the reasoning that a job description strips out.
Five questions to open an interview:
“Tell me about the client you found hardest to keep.”
“Which decision would you make differently today?”
“Which supplier must we never lose, and why?”
“Which house rule is written down nowhere?”
“What does your successor need to know in the first month?”
Documents to gather alongside
Interviews give the reasoning. A few documents give the facts:
leadership meeting minutes from recent years;
key contracts, with a note from the leader on what was negotiated and why;
the history of prices and discounts granted to major clients;
the real organisation chart, the one that shows who actually decides;
an annotated address book: who to call, for what, and what to know beforehand.
These documents feed the assistant just like the interviews. They go through the same review: the leader removes anything that shouldn’t circulate.
How the assistant works
The technique is called retrieval-augmented generation. The assistant “knows” nothing on its own: for each question, it searches the leader’s notes for the relevant passages, then writes its answer from those passages only, and cites them.
For the successor, the citation makes all the difference. They can see where the answer comes from, reread the original interview and judge for themselves.
One question, end to end
Take a typical question from the successor: “Why do we still use this carrier when a competitor is cheaper?”
The assistant searches the interviews. It finds the passage where the leader tells the story of a delivery saved one evening in a crisis, and the loyalty commitment made afterwards. It answers in two sentences and points to the original interview, with its date.
If no interview covers the subject, it says so. The successor then knows to ask the leader, while they are still there. That silence is useful: it shows what the memory is missing.
The leader edits their own memory
Nothing goes into the assistant without their approval. They review the transcripts, remove what they don’t want passed on, correct what was misunderstood.
This step also reassures those who hesitate to open up. People speak more freely when they know they will review everything.
Who runs the project
The leader provides the material. They can’t carry it alone: they are still running the company.
Four roles are enough in an SME:
the leader, who tells, reviews and approves;
the successor, who asks the questions and tests the assistant;
an internal coordinator, often the executive assistant, who schedules the interviews and follows up the reviews;
the IT lead or an outside provider, for the tool, the access rights and security.
The internal coordinator knows the leader’s diary and files. They are also the person who can find an hour in an already full week.
What the law says
Recorded interviews are personal data: the leader’s voice, their opinions, sometimes the names of clients or employees. The GDPR applies: inform, obtain the leader’s consent, limit retention, protect access.
People mentioned in the interviews have rights too. The simplest rule: anonymise client and employee names before feeding the assistant, unless there is a real need.
Under the AI Act, an internal assistant of this kind is not a high-risk system, as long as it isn’t used to assess or manage employees. The transparency rule in force since 2 August 2026 is easy to meet: everyone knows they are asking an AI.
Where to keep this memory
This knowledge is strategic. It has no place in a consumer tool that might use it to train its models. Choose a business plan that excludes this by contract, ideally hosted in Europe, with named user access.
Ask the ownership question too: if the company is sold, is the digital twin part of the sale? Better to write it into the sale agreement than to find out after signing.
What the buyer gains
A buyer acquires accounts, contracts and teams. They also acquire a risk: not understanding what holds the whole thing together.
A documented memory reduces that risk. It shows why clients stay, how prices were set, which decisions failed. It reassures the buyer and eases the first months, when losing a key client is costly.
Prepare it like the rest of the sale file: who has access, what it contains, what was removed from it.
Check that it works
Before relying on the assistant, test it:
prepare twenty real questions, asked by the successor and two managers;
check that every answer cites an interview, and that the quote says what the assistant claims;
note the questions left unanswered: those are the interviews to hold first;
repeat the test every quarter, with new questions.
An assistant that answers eighteen questions out of twenty correctly, and admits it doesn’t know the other two, is ready to use. An assistant that answers everything isn’t.
Mistakes to avoid
Five mistakes come up often:
recording everything without sorting, and drowning what matters;
picking a consumer tool to save time;
skipping the leader’s review;
mistaking a document archive for an assistant that answers;
starting three months before the sale.
The last one is the most common. The only fix is to start earlier.
When to start
Several years before leaving, a leader still has the time and the distance to tell the story. A few months before a sale, urgency takes over: negotiation, audits, announcing it to the team.
France’s proposed “Papin pact”, included in the 2027 draft budget for sales between 2027 and 2029, has yet to be voted. If it passes, it will speed up handovers. Knowledge can’t be caught up in a few weeks.
Three signs it is time to start
Don’t wait for a departure date to begin:
the leader is the only one who can answer certain client questions;
a sale, a family handover or opening up the capital is being discussed, even vaguely;
teams say “we’ll have to ask the boss” several times a week.
One of these signs is enough. Each shows that part of the company’s value sits in a single head.
After the leader leaves
The memory doesn’t stop on the day the leader leaves. In the first months, the successor turns to it often. Then the questions change: the company moves on, new decisions are added.
Decide in advance who keeps it up to date, who can access it and how long it is kept. The former leader may agree to be contacted to fill a gap, over a period agreed together. Put it in writing, like everything else.
Over time, the leader’s memory becomes the company’s. That is the real goal: knowledge that belongs to the business, not to one person.
A project on a human scale
No big IT programme is needed. Ten one-hour interviews, as many reviews and a few weeks of set-up are enough for a first version.
The hard part isn’t the tool. It is blocking one hour a week in the leader’s diary to tell the story. That is where the project succeeds or fails.
What I advise leaders
A five-step approach, with no big budget:
list the ten decisions that shaped the company most;
give each one a one-hour interview, recorded with the leader’s consent;
have the leader review and correct every transcript;
test the assistant with the future successor, on real questions;
add to the memory every quarter until departure.
Keeping a leader’s knowledge is a governance matter more than an IT one. That memory protects the company’s value as much as its price.
AI can keep a leader’s memory. Choosing what deserves to be passed on remains theirs.
Valérie Mailland
Founder of EXEC'IA Consulting. 20+ years alongside executives, including 18 in executive coordination at McKinsey & Company. Follow me on LinkedIn →

## More AI tools, not more impact
URL : https://exec-ia.ai/perspective-probleme-nest-pas-outils-mais-arbitrage-en.html

← All articles Blog • Value creation
More AI tools do not
mean more impact.
It is not a tools problem.
It is a trade-off problem.
Article developed from my LinkedIn post (9 September 2026)
Updated on 1 October 2026
Short version →
Heads of communications: more AI tools do not mean more impact. It is a question of choosing, not of tools.
Three questions are enough to sort them: is there a real challenge?
A named budget and owner?
Could you stop it tomorrow without regret?
Without that sorting, a team ends up running five projects halfway rather than two all the way. Gartner even predicted that 30% of generative AI projects would be abandoned for lack of clear business value.
The ritual that prevents this drift: a short review every quarter, where each tool has to justify its place.
You run your company’s communications?
You know the reflex: as soon as a new AI tool comes out, you try it. Then another. Then another.
Coordinating communications for the McKinsey France Alumni network, I saw how easy it is to add one more tool. And how rare it is to take the time to ask which one matters.
There is nothing careless about that reflex. Every new tool promises to succeed where the last one failed. And refusing to try it feels like falling behind. The pressure is real, fuelled by the speed at which new versions come out.
The problem is not the tools. It is choosing between them.
A Gartner study predicted that 30% of generative AI projects would be abandoned after the first trial, for lack of clear business value. That figure does not mean these projects were technically poor. It means they were never tied to a challenge clear enough to see them through.
A more recent survey points the same way. Published by Gartner in April 2026 and covering 782 IT infrastructure and operations leaders, it shows that only 28% of AI use cases fully meet their return-on-investment expectations, and that 20% fail outright, most often because they were too ambitious or poorly scoped.
The easiest symptom to spot?
A team that can name the last five tools it tested without hesitating, but struggles to say which one changed anything measurable. It is not a lack of curiosity. It is a missing filter between trying and adopting.
🛠️ Why do more AI tools not mean more impact?
Because more tools means more dispersion. And a team running five projects halfway, rather than two all the way.
🎯 What three criteria decide which AI tool is worth keeping?
A real brand, crisis or launch challenge, not a trend to follow?
A committed budget and a named owner ready to decide, not just to watch?
A tool you could switch off tomorrow morning without anyone missing it?
Why these three criteria specifically?
Because each one removes a trap.
The first rules out passing fads: testing a tool because a competitor uses it is not a challenge, it is a comparison.
The second forces a decision: without a budget or a named owner, a tool stays a trial, never a choice.
The third protects you from money already spent: a tool you no longer dare to stop, because of the time it took to set up, ends up costing more than the one you never launched.
Who should carry this trade-off role on a small team?
On a small communications team, there is no need for a new job. It is enough for one person, often the one already managing the budget or the schedule, to be clearly tasked with applying the three criteria to any new tool, before it settles in.
Day to day, it changes almost nothing, except at one precise moment: when someone suggests trying a new tool. Then one question is enough: which real need does it meet that our current tools do not?
If nobody asks that question, every tool settles in by default, without anyone choosing it. The risk is not that a bad tool takes over. It is that ten average tools live side by side, each half-covering a need another already covers.
Three projects seen through beat fifteen moving in parallel without ever landing.
AI can show you many options. It will never choose for you.
What separates a tool you keep from one you tolerate?
A tool you keep clearly meets the three criteria: a named challenge, an assumed budget, a person ready to answer for it in front of the team. A tool you tolerate usually meets none of them. It was tried once, nobody decided to stop it, and it keeps running in the background, eating team time without anyone having chosen it.
The difference does not show in the tool. It shows when you ask the team: why this one rather than another?
If the answer is slow to come, no choice was ever made. The tool stayed out of habit. Try it at your next team meeting: pick a tool at random and ask the person using it to say, in one sentence, which result it changed.
What happens when no one decides?
In practice, one obstacle keeps coming up: nobody is clearly tasked with sorting. Everyone keeps the tool they tested, because they put time into it and do not want to see it dropped. Without someone whose role it is, and who is attached to no tool in particular, the list only grows. Nobody decides not to decide. The list simply grows while everyone waits for someone else to deal with it.
Deciding also means accepting that a dropped tool is not a failure. It is proof the sorting worked. A team that never drops anything has probably never sorted.
How do you apply this sorting day to day?
Sorting works better as a ritual than as a big decision: a short review every quarter, where each active tool has to justify its place against the three criteria. Whatever no longer passes is stopped, without a long debate.
That rhythm avoids the most common trap: waiting for the big annual clean-up, by which time the list has already doubled. A short, regular ritual takes less energy. Above all, it stops the list from ever getting long enough to need a big clean-up.
How do you introduce this ritual without adding a new burden?
By keeping it short. Fifteen minutes are enough if each tool goes through the same three criteria, always in the same order. What makes it heavy is not how often it happens. It is the temptation to add new criteria each time. Three stable criteria, applied without exception, beat ten criteria adjusted case by case.
The sign it works?
Not the number of tools removed. It is that the list of active tools stops growing on its own between two reviews.
💬 In your communications, how many
AI initiatives
are moving forward, and how many never get finished?
Sources: Gartner, “Predicts 30% of Generative AI Projects Will Be Abandoned After Proof of Concept By End of 2025”, 2024; Gartner, “Gartner Says AI Projects in I&O Stall Ahead of Meaningful ROI Returns”, 7 April 2026.
#ArtificialIntelligence #Communications #ValueCreation #AIStrategy
Going further
Four more questions to take the thinking further.
Read the full articleabout 3,000 words→
Mapping your tools in one hour
Before sorting, you need to see. Many teams discover they do not know how many tools are running, who pays for them, or who uses them.
A five-column table is enough:
the tool, and the need it covers, in one sentence;
the person who uses it most, and the one who answers for it;
the cost, subscription and time to learn included;
the date it was last really used;
the date of the next review.
This table often reveals duplicates: three writing tools, two image generators, one transcription app paid for by two people. The sorting then starts on its own.
How do you say yes to a new tool?
With a short trial whose rules everyone knows. One person, one precise use, thirty days, one indicator chosen in advance.
At the end of the month, three possible outcomes: the tool joins the list, it replaces an existing tool, or it stops. The trial commits you to nothing and does not settle in by default. This framework makes yes easier, because it makes no less painful.
The trap of AI features you already have
Before buying a new tool, one check often saves a subscription: the office suite, design tool or customer relationship software you already pay for may offer the same feature.
These built-in features are sometimes less spectacular. But they have one big advantage: they live inside tools the team already knows, with the security rules already in place.
What about free tools?
Free does not mean no cost. You often pay in learning time, in data handed over, and in terms of use that can change overnight.
A free tool can be used to test an idea. It should never receive confidential information, or become a working tool without going through the same review as the others.
Why piling up tools damages the brand
In communications, dispersion has a cost other functions know less well: consistency. Every tool has its own habits of tone, its turns of phrase, its visual style.
When five people produce with five different tools, the brand ends up speaking with five voices. Readers do not know why, but they feel something no longer fits. Reducing the number of tools is also about protecting an identity.
How do you keep a brand voice with AI?
Three simple rules, shared by all the tools you keep:
a short style guide, with the tone, the words to use and the ones to avoid, given to the tool at the start of every task;
examples of successful texts, which show the expected voice better than an abstract instruction;
a human review before any publication, by someone who knows the brand.
The fewer tools there are, the easier these rules are to keep. With two tools, you master them. With ten, you give up.
What about generated images?
Here I would be especially careful. An image produced by a tool can reuse, without saying so, elements close to protected works, or the face of a real person.
Before publishing, three checks: do the tool’s terms allow commercial use?
Does the image imitate a recognisable style or work?
Does it show an identifiable person?
When in doubt, legal advice costs less than a complaint.
Depth rather than breadth
A team that masters two tools often produces better work than a team that skims ten. Mastery comes with time: refined instructions, known mistakes, learned shortcuts.
Every new tool resets that counter to zero. One more reason to choose few, and to go deep on what you chose.
What do you do when a vendor changes its prices or terms?
It happens often, and fast. A free tool becomes paid, a feature disappears, the rules on data change.
A team that depends on ten tools goes through these changes ten times. A team that chose two can follow them closely and prepare a fallback. Two precautions help: check that you can export your content easily, and keep a record of the instructions that work, so you can reuse them elsewhere if needed.
AI in crisis communications
A crisis is the worst moment to discover a tool’s limits. Answers must be accurate, dated, approved, and sometimes reviewed by a lawyer.
AI can help prepare key messages, summarise what is being said or translate a statement. It must never publish on its own, or reply directly to a journalist or an angry customer. Set that rule in a calm moment, before the crisis: you will not have to improvise it at the worst time.
How do you involve agencies and suppliers?
By sharing with them the list of tools you kept and your brand rules. An agency using its own tools without knowing your choices brings back the dispersion you have just reduced.
One conversation at the start of the collaboration is often enough: which tools do you use, for what, and how do you respect our guidelines?
It saves plenty of last-minute corrections.
Which indicators should a communications team track?
Three simple measures show whether the tools are useful:
the time between a request and publication;
the number of approval rounds per piece of content;
the share of content published without substantive correction.
If these figures do not move after a tool arrives, the tool takes time without giving any back. That is an objective argument for deciding at the quarterly review.
And when the tool comes from the CEO?
Sometimes a tool is chosen at the top, because a leader saw it at a peer’s company or at a trade show. It deserves the same review as the others, no more, no less.
Applying the three criteria to a tool that came from the top is not disloyal. It is doing leadership a favour: they want a result, not one more tool. Presented that way, the sorting is almost always well received.
A typical example
Take a five-person communications team that built up about ten tools in a year. The map shows three writing tools, two image generators, two transcription tools and several forgotten trials.
After a review, the team keeps one writing tool, one image tool and one transcription tool, and stops the rest. It trains everyone on those three tools, writes its style guide and sets its next review. Three months later, it produces as much, with lower costs, a more consistent voice and a less scattered team.
What choosing sets free
Choosing few tools does not shrink ambition. It frees attention for what gives a communications team its value: the message, judgement, the relationship with audiences.
The tool remains a means. Strategy remains your job.
How do you avoid piling up tools?
→
With a simple rule: no new tool without a named use, an owner and a review date. A tool with no owner ends up serving nobody, while it keeps costing money.
When a new tool arrives, ask the right question: which tool does it replace, or which use does it make unnecessary?
This discipline also protects the budget. Every tool withdrawn frees up a subscription, training time and attention for the ones that remain.
Once a year, list the tools you pay for against how they are actually used. You will often find two teams paying for the same need.
The right reflex: every new subscription goes through the same person, who checks it does not duplicate an existing one.
How do you properly retire a tool that is no longer used?
→
Set a date, warn the people who use it, and recover what needs recovering: data, templates, good habits. Stopping a tool is prepared like a launch, only shorter.
A team that knows how to stop dares to test more, because it knows a trial does not commit it forever.
Warning people a few weeks ahead, and letting everyone export their work, avoids most of the frustration.
Write down why you stopped it. It will stop the same tool coming back in a year, under another name or through another team.
Think about the vendor too: many subscriptions renew automatically, often for a full year. Put the cancellation date in the diary.
What does the choosing itself cost?
→
Very little money, a little time. A monthly review of a few uses is often enough, with someone who has the power to say yes or no. What is expensive is not doing it: scattered projects that never land.
Sorting is an investment of attention, not an extra budget.
The simplest way: give this meeting to the person who already sets the team’s priorities. The ritual then slips into time that already exists.
For an SME, one hour a month around a shared table of current uses is usually enough to get started.
The real cost is the courage to say no to a tool someone likes. That is why you need a person who clearly has that power.
How do you help a team say no to a good tool?
→
By reminding them the question is not how good the tool is. It is how useful it is for a specific challenge, right now. An excellent tool that serves no priority need waits its turn, and the team is allowed to like it.
Saying no at that moment is what lets you say a stronger yes to what matters.
Put the answer in writing: it will serve as a reference the next time the tool comes back into the conversation.
Also suggest adding the tool to a waiting list, with the condition that would make it a priority. The no becomes a “not now”, which is far easier to accept.
Valérie Mailland
Founder of EXEC'IA Consulting. 20+ years alongside executives, including 18 in executive coordination at McKinsey & Company. Follow me on LinkedIn →

## Can your AI project be funded?
URL : https://exec-ia.ai/perspective-projet-ia-peut-il-etre-finance-en.html

← All articles Blog • Funding
Can your AI project be funded?
Yes, but not necessarily
the one you have in mind.
Article developed from my LinkedIn post (25 September 2026) · Updated on October 6, 2026
Short version →
SME leaders: yes, an AI project can be funded. But not necessarily yours, not in every company, and not for every kind of service.
The Diag Data IA scheme funds a technical analysis, carried out by an approved expert.
The Osez l’IA plan lists ready-made solutions and approved experts. Not open consulting.
A subsidy should never decide your project: first the problem to solve, then the funding.
You run an SME and you wonder whether your AI project could be funded?
This piece is for you.
It all started with an audit of my site’s visibility on Google and in AI answers. One question came up: what are my future clients actually asking themselves?
Among them: “Is there any funding for my AI project?” Good question. So I went and took a closer look.
Osez l’IA, France 2030, Bpifrance, Diag Data IA, France Num, regional schemes… The funding exists. But behind the word “support”, the realities are very different: eligible company or not, fundable service or not, free choice of provider or imposed, share covered, amount left to pay.
💶 Should funding determine your AI project?
No, never. I always keep this order:
what problem do you want to solve?
Where can AI really create value?
Which project should be prioritised?
And only then: which schemes may apply?
A project built to fit a scheme risks solving no real problem.
You would then have spent time, and part of the money, on a result nobody was waiting for. Funding should speed up a project you have already chosen, never choose it for you.
What does Diag Data IA fund?
For SMEs and mid-sized companies with 10 to 2,000 employees, Bpifrance’s IA Booster programme, part of France 2030, first offers free awareness sessions. Then a Diag Data IA co-funded at 40%: €10,000 excl. VAT, of which €6,000 excl. VAT is paid by the company.
It is a technical diagnosis, carried out by a Bpifrance-approved expert. Conditions apply, including turnover of at least €1M and being an independent company.
So you do not freely choose the provider. And this diagnosis does not replace the strategic thinking upstream: which use to prioritise, and why that one.
Which main families of support exist for an AI project?
There are three, each with its own logic.
Diagnostic schemes fund an analysis, such as the Diag Data IA.
Solution catalogues list ready-to-use products, such as one of the two strands of the Osez l’IA plan.
Broader support, national or regional, backs digital transformation or investment.
They do not replace one another. Confusing a funded diagnosis with a funded rollout is one of the most common mistakes.
Before filling in an application, check which family it belongs to: that tells you what will really be funded, and what will stay at your expense.
Why is the provider question decisive?
Because, depending on the scheme, you either choose your provider freely, or they come from a list.
In the first case, you pick the one who understands your business.
In the second, the choice is framed: check that the proposed provider meets your need.
Funding obtained for a provider who does not fit the project costs you time, even when it costs you no money.
How do you combine a funded diagnosis with a strategic project?
By keeping each in its place. The technical diagnosis shows what is possible with your data and your tools. The strategic thinking decides what is worth doing, in what order, with what means.
Ideally, strategy comes first. A diagnosis targeted on a use already chosen brings far more than a general diagnosis with no precise question.
Should you wait for funding before starting?
Not necessarily. Waiting for support can delay by several months a project whose value is already clear. Meanwhile, the problem stays untouched.
The right question is not “support or no support”. It is: “what first step can I take right now, whatever the support?”.
A modest first use, on a precise task, teaches you things no application file can. It also makes the next step easier to defend, including in front of a funding body.
Does “Osez l’IA” fund any kind of consulting?
No. The national Osez l’IA plan has two strands.
The first is a catalogue of ready-to-use AI solutions for SMEs and mid-sized companies: assistants, automation, document analysis. These are products.
The second groups support programmes run by Bpifrance, such as the Diag Data IA and the AI Accelerator, delivered by approved experts.
In both cases, you do not freely choose the provider. A strategic scoping workshop such as Cap IA is neither a catalogue product nor an approved-expert service: it does not fall under these schemes, and I do not present it as fundable by them.
EXEC’IA’s AI Agents, on the other hand, are product solutions: SENTRY, ECHO or RELAY could fit into a catalogue of this kind, provided they are selected.
Which questions should you ask before filing an application?
Five checks save you from unpleasant surprises:
is your company eligible (size, turnover, sector)?
Is the intended service fundable?
Can you freely choose your provider, or is it imposed?
What is the funding rate?
What is the out-of-pocket cost, and for what result?
The exact conditions are published by the bodies themselves (France Num, Bpifrance, entreprises.gouv.fr), and they change. Check them at the source, when you apply.
Where do you start, in practice?
With the problem, not the funding desk.
Write down what AI should change in your business, find where it creates value, choose a first project.
Funding comes next, based on that project.
Funding and compliance should both be anticipated at the scoping stage: for the second, see the AI Act and GDPR guide for an SME.
Which mistakes should you avoid when looking for support?
Five mistakes come up again and again:
building a project to fit a scheme,
ignoring the out-of-pocket cost,
confusing diagnosis and deployment,
forgetting compliance (AI Act, GDPR) at the scoping stage, and
starting too late.
The last one deserves checking every time: depending on the scheme, the application sometimes has to be made before the service starts. It is written in the official conditions. Read them before committing.
What if your company is not eligible?
Do not give up on the project.
An ineligible company can fund a first use itself, starting small: one task, one team, one measurable result.
It is even the best way to find out whether the project deserves a bigger investment.
Having no support is not a verdict on the project’s value.
It only changes the pace and the size of the first step.
How do you keep your bearings?
Among so many schemes
By coming back to the starting question: what problem do you want to solve?
Schemes are many, their conditions change, and so does their vocabulary.
Your problem stays the same. That is what should guide the choice.
A leader who knows which problem they want to solve reads a list of funding schemes as a list of options.
One who does not know yet reads it as a list of constraints.
Which three things should you keep in mind?
The project must exist without the support, even on a smaller scale.
Conditions are checked at the source, on the date you apply.
Compliance is thought through from the start, not after the rollout.
If these three points are settled, the support becomes what it should be:
an accelerator for a project already chosen, not the reason for choosing it.
What place for strategic support before funding?
A place upstream, to answer a question funding schemes rarely address:
where can AI create value in your company, and where do you start?
That is the role of a scoping workshop such as Cap IA at EXEC’IA.
Once the problem and the priority are clear, the funded diagnosis, the chosen solution and any support fall into place much more simply.
You choose with a clear direction, instead of picking from a menu.
How do you present your project to a funding body?
Problem before solution: what you want to change, for whom, and how you will know it worked.
A funding body pays for an expected result more than for an intention.
An application built on a clear need, a limited scope and a simple success criterion is quicker to read and easier to defend.
Also prepare your answers to three questions: who will carry the project internally, how much time it will take, and what you will do if the result disappoints.
Those answers reassure as much as a figure.
What do you do once the funding is granted?
Funding pays for a step, not for what follows.
Plan from the start for what happens next: who uses the result, who develops it, and how you decide to continue.
A diagnosis left in a drawer changes nothing in the business.
Go back to the starting order: problem, value, priority. It will tell you whether the funded step was the right one, and what the next one is.
Keep every document too: invoices, deliverables, meeting notes. A funding body may ask for them, sometimes months later.
💬 Before investing in an AI project, would you
think to check which support you may claim?
Source: France Num, IA Booster · France Num, Diag Data IA · entreprises.gouv.fr. Conditions checked on October 6, 2026, to be re-checked at the time of application.
#ArtificialIntelligence #SME #Bpifrance #France2030 #OsezLIA #EXECIA #BlogEXECIA
Read the full articleabout 3,000 words→
What a first project really costs
Before looking for funding, you need to know what you want to fund. The listed price of a tool is often only part of the spending.
Six items make up the real budget of a first project:
scoping, to choose the use and set the indicator;
licences or subscriptions, for the planned number of users;
connection to existing tools, where needed;
team training, at the start and over time;
human review time, as long as the tool can get things wrong;
internal time spent on the project, by the leader and the teams.
The last item is the one most often forgotten. Yet it weighs the most in an SME: every hour spent on the project is an hour taken from somewhere else.
How do you estimate a project’s return, simply?
By comparing two figures over one year: what the project costs in total, and what it earns or saves, measured on the indicator chosen at the start.
For a leader, a payback period often speaks louder than a percentage: after how many months has the project paid back what it cost?
If the answer is longer than the tool’s likely lifespan, rethink the project before funding it.
Training, often easier to fund than the tool
It is an option people often forget. In France, staff training can be covered by the company’s skills operator, the OPCO, depending on its size and the rules of its sector.
Training is often the key to getting a tool adopted. Funding skills first, then the tool, is also the order that works best: teams that understand what they are going to use, and why.
What about regional support?
Several French regions support the digital transformation of small businesses and SMEs: vouchers, grants, interest-free loans or group programmes. Conditions differ from one region to another, and change often.
The chamber of commerce, the regional economic development agency or your local France Num adviser usually know what is open at the time you call. Fifteen minutes on the phone saves hours of searching.
Are tax credits a good fit?
Rarely for simply using a tool. Research and innovation tax credits target design and development work, not the purchase of off-the-shelf software.
They can make sense if the company develops a new solution itself, for example a custom tool built on its own data. In that case, ask your accountant before you start: you will avoid unpleasant surprises in an audit.
Subscription or investment?
The question looks like accounting. In reality, it is strategic. A subscription is paid monthly, easy to stop and counts as an expense. Custom development needs an upfront investment, but can become a company asset.
For a first project, a subscription is often the wisest choice: it lets you test at a controlled cost, and stop if the use does not deliver. Investment makes sense once the use is proven.
Should you involve your accountant?
Yes, and early. Several practical questions are theirs, and they are easier to settle before the first invoice than after.
Three examples come up often:
subscriptions billed by foreign vendors, for which VAT is usually self-assessed by the French company;
how spending is recorded, as an expense or as an asset, depending on whether it is a subscription or a development;
possible eligibility for a tax credit, which depends on the real nature of the work.
Half an hour is often enough. It avoids costly corrections, and gives you a clear view of what the project really costs, tax included.
Subscriptions in dollars
Many AI tools are billed in dollars. The amount in euros therefore moves with the exchange rate, and the bank may add fees to every payment.
For an annual budget, allow a margin of a few per cent. Some vendors offer billing in euros or an annual payment: simpler to manage, and often cheaper overall.
What about several companies together?
It is an underrated route. Business clubs, trade federations and chambers of commerce sometimes run group programmes: workshops, shared diagnoses, small-group training.
The cost per company goes down, and talking with leaders facing the same questions is often worth as much as the content itself. For a small business, it is an accessible first step before a project of its own.
How do you present a convincing application?
Whether for a public body, a bank or your own executive committee, four elements are often enough:
the problem to solve, described with the company’s own figures;
the use chosen, and why that one rather than another;
the indicator that will judge the result;
the full budget and the timeline, with the decision points.
An application that is clear on these four points stands out straight away. Most requests describe a tool. Few describe the expected result.
Beware of “free” offers paid for by a vendor
Some offers present themselves as free or funded, when their main purpose is to install a solution that is hard to leave afterwards. The cost comes later, at renewal or the day you want to switch tools.
Before accepting, three questions are enough: what happens when the free period ends?
Can the data be retrieved easily?
Does the tool answer the priority problem?
Timelines, a factor to plan for
Public schemes have processing times that can take several weeks. Some require the application to be filed before anything starts.
The right reflex: run both in parallel. Prepare the application while you refine the scoping, without committing any spending that would make the project ineligible. The funding timeline should not dictate the project’s timeline, but you should not discover it too late either.
What if the application is turned down?
Do not conclude that the project is bad. A refusal often comes down to an administrative criterion: company size, sector, timing, a budget already used up.
Ask for the exact reason. If it is about the application, it tells you what to clarify. If it is about eligibility, it invites you to look for another scheme, or to fund a modest first step yourself, whose results will make the next application stronger.
A well-understood refusal often saves time: it forces you to pin down the problem, the indicator and the budget. That is exactly what the project needed anyway.
A typical example
Take a thirty-person SME that wants to cut the time spent preparing quotes. After a short scoping, it chooses a precise use, sets an indicator, the average response time, and works out its full budget.
It gets the sales team’s training funded by its OPCO, takes out a subscription for a three-month trial, and prepares in parallel an application to its region for the next step. Three months later, it has real figures: the next step is easier to fund, and easier to decide.
What to remember
Funding follows clarity, never the other way round. A company that knows which problem it wants to solve, with which indicator and which budget, finds the right schemes more easily, and above all the right partners.
One that looks for funding first, then a project to justify it, loses time for an uncertain result. The order matters more than the amount.
Valérie Mailland
Founder of EXEC'IA Consulting. 20+ years alongside executives, including 18 in executive coordination at McKinsey & Company. Follow me on LinkedIn →

Adopting AI is one thing. Creating value from it is another.

## Humanoid robots and the token tax: which tasks go first
URL : https://exec-ia.ai/perspective-robots-humanoides-token-tax-en.html

← All articles Blog • Humanoid robots
Humanoid robots: which tasks
will go first?
October 6, 2026 · Updated on October 6, 2026
Short version →
Employees, managers, business leaders: a humanoid robot takes over tasks, rarely a whole job.
France’s labour statistics office, Dares, counts 457,500 vacancies in the private sector in Q2 2026. Humanoids will go first for those hard-to-fill roles: carrying, sorting, storing, night work.
Two questions reach beyond the company: who builds these robots, and who pays for social protection when part of the work no longer runs through wages? The “token tax” has entered the debate.
The mini-diagnostic in this article measures, in two minutes, how much of your week could go to a robot.
You run an SME, you lead a team, or you wonder what will become of your own role?
This article is for you.
A humanoid robot will not take your job in one go. It will chip away at it, task by task. The real question is which tasks, and in what order.
A Reel on French news channel LCI recently mentioned 300,000 unfilled positions in France. The country’s labour statistics office, Dares, counts more: 457,500 vacancies in the private sector in Q2 2026, according to its revised figure of September 15.
A vacancy is not always a role nobody can fill. Dares includes unoccupied positions, newly created ones and positions about to become free. So the figure does not say “this many people are missing”. It says: a lot of companies are hiring, right now.
🔑 Why think in tasks rather than jobs?
Because a job is a bundle. An order picker moves crates, but also spots a labelling error, reassures a customer on the phone, trains a temp. A robot can take over the first task. The others call for judgement, relationships and accountability.
Thinking in jobs leads to two opposite mistakes: believing nothing will change, or believing everything will disappear. Thinking in tasks shows what is really shifting, role by role.
Which jobs will humanoid robots target first?
Those where tasks are physical, repetitive or strenuous, in places designed for people: warehouses, workshops, shop stockrooms, building sites, farms, and healthcare settings for moving equipment around.
These are often the hardest roles to fill. The robot does not come first to take a seat that is occupied. It comes to cover a role the company cannot fill: night shifts, heavy handling, hazardous tasks.
Three questions to ask for every role:
Which tasks could a robot take over?
What will the job become without them?
Which vacant role around you could a robot cover?
Why is none of this imminent?
The excitement is real, the reality slower. Even Apple is not expected to mass-produce its robots before 2028, according to analyst Ming-Chi Kuo. Today’s humanoids remain expensive, slow at movements people make without thinking, and fragile when the unexpected happens.
So the timeline gives you some breathing room. Use it to prepare, not to wait.
What is the good news for those who keep their jobs?
A robot produces without a salary, without overtime and without an annual raise. Once paid off, it becomes a predictable cost, which can hold back part of the price increases.
On one condition: the time freed up must go to more useful and more interesting work, not to piling on more. That is a leadership choice, not an automatic effect.
Who builds these robots?
In the first half of 2026, 97% of the humanoid robots delivered worldwide came out of Chinese factories. The two leading makers, AgiBot and Unitree, are Chinese.
Which raises a question for France and for Europe: design and run our own robots, or buy them off the shelf, together with the data they collect in our workshops and warehouses. For an SME, it is also a practical question: who will handle maintenance, spare parts and updates?
Who pays for social protection?
In France, pensions and social protection rely largely on contributions levied on wages. A robot pays none, and it is written off as an expense.
Bill Gates put it plainly in a long essay published at the end of August 2026: when you hire someone, you pay payroll taxes; when you buy a robot, you can often write it off right away. Without meaning to, the tax system nudges companies to replace people with machines.
What is the “token tax”?
A token is the unit of text that AI models process, and the unit they bill for every request. The idea is to levy a small percentage on those tokens, in other words on the use of AI, rather than only on the profits of the companies that build it.
Where does the debate stand?
1) Bill Gates argues for taxing AI tokens and robots.
2) In the United States, a bill introduced in Congress in August 2026, the AI Tax and Work Protection Act, proposes a 2% rate on the value of tokens when unemployment is at 5% or below, rising as unemployment rises.
3) The revenue would fund jobs and retraining. Some see it as the basis for a universal income.
The idea is not new. As early as 2017, France and the European Parliament were debating a tax on robots. What has changed is the base: the use of AI can now be measured down to the token.
What can an SME do right now?
🎯 Three steps, without spending a cent.
1) List the tasks in each role and the time they take.
2) Identify the hard-to-fill roles, and what makes them strenuous.
3) Decide what must stay human, before the question is forced on you.
The mini-diagnostic below takes the first step with you, in two minutes.
💬 Taxing AI to protect
those who lose their work:
a good idea, or a brake on our companies?

Read the full articleabout 3,000 words→
What a humanoid robot is, in 2026
A humanoid robot is a machine shaped like a person: two arms, hands, often two legs, a head carrying cameras. It combines three building blocks. A mechanical body, sensors that perceive the surroundings, and an AI “brain” that decides which movement to make.
That last part is what has changed. For decades, an industrial robot repeated a movement programmed to the millimetre, inside a cage, never straying from it. Recent AI models let a humanoid learn a movement by demonstration, recognise an object it has never seen and adapt when a part has been slightly moved.
Why a human shape?
Because our workplaces are built for people. Stairs, handles, shelves, trolleys and tools were all designed for our hands and our height. A human-shaped robot can, in theory, slip into them without anyone rebuilding the warehouse or the workshop.
That is also its limit. In a space designed for it, a specialised robot, a fixed arm or an autonomous trolley often does better and costs less. The humanoid makes sense where the environment changes, where tasks vary, and where nobody wants to refit everything.
What they can do, and what they cannot yet
Today, the most advanced humanoids can:
move and store crates or parcels;
feed a machine or a production line;
carry out simple visual checks;
take stock in a familiar place.
They still struggle with what a person does effortlessly: gripping something soft or slippery, finding their way in a cluttered space, understanding an ambiguous instruction, reacting to the unexpected. Their battery life is often counted in hours, and their pace stays below that of a trained operator.
A headline from Euronews at the end of September 2026 sums it up: the excitement around humanoids is running into reality. The promise is strong; large-scale deployment will take years.
The real economics
A robot does not just cost its purchase price. Add integration on site, safety measures around it, maintenance, spare parts, software updates, training for the staff who supervise it, and downtime when it breaks down.
Many manufacturers now offer pay-per-use rental, on a “robot as a service” model: a monthly subscription, maintenance included. For an SME, it is often the only sensible way to test without tying up capital it will never recover.
So the right question is not “how much does a robot cost?” but “how much does one hour of a task cost, compared with one hour of human work, at the same quality?” Until that calculation is done task by task, every decision is a gamble.
The body and the brain
Robots are often described as a mechanical revolution. They are first an AI revolution. The body is improving, but what changes the game is the robot’s ability to understand what it sees and to choose a movement.
For a business leader, that is good news: the questions to ask are the same as for any AI software tool. Which task, which data, which human oversight, who is accountable when it gets it wrong. The only difference is that here, a mistake can hurt someone.
Sector by sector
Logistics. The most advanced ground: moving crates, picking orders, loading trolleys. Recent warehouses are already highly automated; humanoids target older sites, where nobody wants to rebuild everything.
Manufacturing. Feeding a machine, moving parts at the end of the line, carrying out a visual check. Night work and strenuous roles come first.
Health and care. Carrying linen, meals and equipment, helping with certain movements. Care, listening and human contact stay human. Bill Gates even suggests reserving some jobs, such as caring for older people, for humans, even once machines are able to do them.
Construction, retail, agriculture. Carrying loads, clearing a site, restocking shelves at night, weeding, picking certain crops. Each time, it is the repetitive and strenuous movements that go first, rarely the know-how.
What changes for employees
When a task goes, the job does not necessarily disappear. It is reshaped. The forklift driver who no longer carries becomes the one who supervises three robots, handles incidents and trains newcomers. The order picker becomes the specialist for the complex orders the machine cannot handle.
None of this happens on its own. It takes training, recognition and often a change in pay. Without that, the robot is seen as a threat, and buy-in collapses before the machine is even switched on.
The role of the frontline manager
They are the ones who will see the robot every day. They will know before anyone else whether the machine saves time or wastes it. Involve them from the start: in choosing the tasks, setting up the pilot and defining the safety rules. A manager who was not consulted becomes, without meaning to, the first obstacle.
Safety and the legal framework
A robot moving among employees first raises a safety question. In Europe, the new Machinery Regulation will apply from January 20, 2027, and explicitly covers machines whose behaviour evolves through AI.
The European AI Act classifies as high-risk the AI systems that act as a safety component of a machine. On-board cameras also film people: GDPR applies, with information for employees and limits on the data kept.
In France, companies with at least 50 employees must consult their works council (CSE) before introducing a new technology that changes working conditions. Better to see it as an opportunity: the moment to explain, to hear concerns and to set the rules before rumour sets them for you.
Sovereignty, in practice
With 97% of worldwide deliveries coming from China in the first half of 2026, sovereignty is anything but abstract. A connected robot collects images, floor plans and work patterns. Where does that data go? Who can update the software, or switch it off?
For an SME, three reflexes are enough to start: ask where the data is hosted, check that the robot can run without a permanent connection, and make sure a local provider handles maintenance. These questions do not turn you into a geopolitics expert. They spare you a dependency you would discover too late.
The “token tax”, in detail
The US bill introduced in August 2026 sets two starting rates when unemployment is at 5% or below: 2% on the value of tokens, 3% on revenue from AI services. The higher unemployment climbs, the higher the rates. The revenue would fund jobs in housing, infrastructure, childcare and elder care.
Bill Gates, for his part, proposes taxing tokens and robots to fund retraining and strengthen safety nets. He also argues for “human-reserved” jobs, which society would choose to keep human even when a machine could do them.
The arguments for:
the tax follows the place where value is created;
it corrects the tax advantage given to machines over people;
it funds the transition as it happens.
The arguments against:
taxing use can slow innovation, especially in small companies;
tokens move easily from one country to another;
the cost may fall on the end user, which means on SMEs themselves.
For a European SME, the stakes are concrete: if such a tax ever comes in, it will be added to the price of the AI tools you use. Better to know now which ones really create value.
And universal income?
The idea returns with every wave of automation. Finland tested it in 2017 and 2018 with two thousand unemployed people: recipients’ well-being improved, while the effect on employment stayed modest. The debate is less about the principle than about the funding. That is exactly where the “token tax” comes in.
Questions to ask a supplier
Before any trial, six simple questions save months:
on which precise tasks has the robot proven itself, and where?
what is its real hourly pace, compared with an operator?
what happens when it does not understand a situation?
where do the images and data it collects go?
who steps in when it breaks down, and how fast?
can the rental be stopped without penalty after the pilot?
A serious supplier answers straight, with figures measured at other customers’ sites. If all you hear about is demonstrations, you know where you stand.
What your teams are wondering
They are not wondering whether the robot performs well. They are wondering what it will change for them: “will I keep my job?”, “will I have to learn to operate it?”, “who is responsible if it gets things wrong?”.
Answer before you are asked. Say clearly which tasks are targeted, which are not, and what will happen to the time freed up. A team that knows the rules accepts a trial far more readily than a team that discovers a robot one Monday morning. The first pilot is also a test of trust: what you do with the time saved will be watched by the whole company.
What I advise an SME leader
A five-step method, with no upfront purchase:
map the tasks of two or three key roles, with the time they take;
flag those that are strenuous, repetitive or hard to staff;
decide with your teams what must stay human;
cost one hour of a robotised task, rental and maintenance included;
if the numbers add up, run a 90-day pilot on a single task.
At the end of the pilot, you will know what the robot brings in your company, not in a manufacturer’s showroom. You will also know how your teams experienced it. That double proof is what lets you decide, or walk away without regret.
A typical example
Take a 60-person logistics SME that can no longer find order pickers for its night shift. Rather than buying a robot, management lists the night-shift tasks: one in two consists of moving crates from one zone to another.
It rents a robot for three months, for that single task, with a volunteer employee in charge of supervising it. At the end of the pilot, the night role stays human, but it changes in nature: less carrying, more checking. Hiring becomes possible again. The robot has not replaced an employee; it has made a role bearable.
What robots really ask of us
Less fascination, more method. Humanoid robots will arrive through tasks, one by one, and first where hands are short. Companies that have mapped their tasks in advance will choose. The others will follow the manufacturers’ timetable.
The question is not whether a robot can do your job. It is deciding, before you invest, what must stay human.
Valérie Mailland
Founder of EXEC'IA Consulting. 20+ years alongside executives, including 18 in executive coordination at McKinsey & Company. Follow me on LinkedIn →
