## Shadow AI: the policy nobody follows
URL : https://exec-ia.ai/perspective-shadow-ia-charte-comite-direction-en.html

← All articles Blog • Shadow AI
An AI policy that its own
leaders do not follow
is no longer a policy.
September 25, 2026 · Updated on October 1, 2026
Short version →
Executive committee members: according to a WalkMe study from July 2025, 78% of employees use AI tools their company has never approved.
A 2025 Cybernews survey adds that 93% of the executives and senior managers surveyed do the same.
To me, the issue is not team discipline. It is the governance around it.
Three reflexes: acknowledge real usage before banning it, offer safe and simple tools, look at the leadership team’s own habits first.
You sit on an executive committee and you have just adopted an AI policy?
This piece is for you.
The policy is drafted in committee. And in the lift afterwards, everyone goes back to their personal AI tool.
A WalkMe study from July 2025 confirms it at scale: 78% of employees use AI tools their company has never approved.
More surprising: according to a 2025 Cybernews survey, 93% of the executives and senior managers surveyed do exactly the same.
On the company side, Gartner reaches the same conclusion: 69% of organisations suspect or have evidence that their teams use unauthorised generative AI.
🔍 Why is shadow AI not a question of discipline?
Because usage is massive, and shared all the way to the top. When almost everyone works around the rule, it is no longer about individuals. It is a sign that the rule does not meet the need.
Punishing will not change anything. As long as the official tool is slower than the personal one, people will make their own choice, quietly.
So the right question becomes: what does the official tool not let people do?
The issue is not team discipline.
It is the governance around it.
An AI policy that its own leaders do not follow is no longer a policy. It is a shared fiction.
What does shadow AI actually hide?
Behind the expression, there are people who want to save time: summarising a document, rewording a message, preparing a meeting. Nothing malicious.
But all of it happens with tools the company has not assessed, and sometimes with information that should never leave the building.
So the risk is not the tool. It is the lack of a clear rule on what can be entrusted to it, and the lack of visibility for leadership.
As long as nobody knows who uses what, nobody can protect the data, or make the most of the good ideas already circulating.
Which data should never leave the company?
Customer information, contracts, personal data, non-public financials and anything covered by business secrecy. A useful policy says so in one simple sentence, with examples everyone recognises from their own work.
On the regulatory side, notably GDPR, an SME that uses AI will find its obligations set out in the AI Act and GDPR guide for an SME.
How do you map usage without hunting for culprits?
By asking in a way that does not punish: which tools save you time, and for which tasks?
A small-group conversation or a short anonymous questionnaire gives a more honest picture than a control exercise.
The goal is to bring real needs to the surface, then answer them with approved tools.
What are the concrete risks of shadow AI?
Three families of risk.
1) An information leak, when a confidential document is pasted into an uncontrolled tool.
2) A decision based on a wrong answer, never reviewed, that then circulates as a fact.
3) A compliance risk, when personal data is processed without a framework.
None of these risks requires malicious intent: they arise from an ordinary gesture, made to save time.
Why do bans so often fail?
Because they leave the need intact.
A person banned from a tool that helps them keeps looking for the same gain elsewhere, out of sight. A ban moves usage into the shadows instead of removing it.
A rule that offers a simple, safe alternative has a far better chance of being followed than one that merely forbids.
Why acknowledge real usage before banning it?
🎯 Which reflexes change the game?
To start, three are enough.
1) Acknowledge real usage.
2) Offer safe and simple tools.
3) Set the example at the top.
Because it already exists, whether we like it or not. Banning a use you do not know about pushes it into the shadows. Mapping it, without hunting for culprits, finally gives an accurate picture of what teams actually do.
How do you offer safe tools that are simpler than the ones people hide?
By providing approved tools that are as quick to pick up as personal ones. If the safe option is heavier than the hidden one, the hidden one wins.
Why start with the leadership team’s own practices?
Because consistency starts at the top. An executive committee that looks honestly at its own usage gives the policy a credibility that no internal memo can replace.
An organisation never secures what it refuses to look at.
What should a useful AI policy contain?
Five elements are often enough.
1) Authorised uses.
2) Forbidden data.
3) Approved tools.
4) A named person to ask questions.
5) A review date.
A two-page policy that everyone has read is worth more than a twenty-page document nobody opens.
It should also be written for those who use it, with their tasks and their words.
How often should it be reviewed?
Regularly, because tools and uses change fast. A quarterly rhythm, with a short item on the executive committee agenda, lets you add an approved tool, remove a use that became risky and check that the rule still matches practice.
A rule frozen for a year describes a situation that no longer exists.
How does a leader set the example?
By applying the policy personally, saying which tools they use and for what, and accepting that the question is put to them.
When executives do what they ask others to do, the rule stops being a constraint and becomes a shared norm.
That is the condition for the policy to stop being a fiction and become a steering tool again.
Where do you start this week?
With a half-hour conversation in the executive committee: which AI tools does each person really use, and with what information?
That frank, judgement-free conversation is worth more than a new version of the policy.
It provides the only solid basis for deciding what to allow, what to offer and what to forbid.
How do you choose which tools to approve?
Start from the real uses found in your company, not from a feature catalogue. Three questions help.
1) What happens to the information entered?
2) Who has access to it?
3) Can people get started with the tool in a few minutes?
It is better to approve a few well-explained tools than to draw up a long list nobody consults.
What role for the legal function or the delegated executive?
A supporting role, not a blocking one. The named contact answers questions quickly, keeps the list of approved tools up to date and alerts the executive committee when a new use appears. Without a fast answer, teams do without the opinion.
In a small organisation, this contact can be the leader personally, provided their availability is known to everyone.
How do you raise awareness without blaming anyone?
By talking about plausible cases rather than faults. A simple example, such as confidential meeting minutes pasted into a consumer tool, is enough to convey the stakes without singling anyone out.
Awareness works better when it comes from the executive committee itself, which acknowledges its own uses before asking others to change theirs.
What should you do about a use that is already in place?
Map it first, without judgement, then decide: keep it if it is safe, replace it with an approved tool if it is not, or frame it with a clear rule.
Plan a transition period so teams do not lose what saves them time.
Announce the change with its reasons. A use withdrawn without explanation almost always reappears elsewhere.
What should you do about information already shared with an unapproved tool?
Assess calmly what may have been shared, without looking for someone to blame. Depending on the nature of the information, notably if it contains personal data, seek legal advice before deciding what to do next.
Note what was learned and build it into the policy: it is the best way to prevent the situation from recurring.
Who should own this topic in the organisation?
A clearly named member of the executive committee, with an operational relay. The subject touches tools, data, human resources and compliance all at once. Without an owner, it is handled piecemeal, and nobody has the full picture.
This owner does not need to be an AI specialist. They must know how to ask the right questions and decide when two needs collide.
In an SME, it is often the leader or their right hand. What matters is that everyone knows who to turn to, and that this person answers quickly.
The same principle applies to every future tool. Each time a new AI service appears on the market, the question will come back: is it approved, for which uses, and with which data?
A policy that answers this question quickly, in writing and in plain words, does more for safety than a long document read once and forgotten. Keeping it short, current and visible is the real discipline, and it is a task that belongs to the leadership team, not only to the people who manage the tools.
💬 And you, do you really know
which AI tools your teams use today?
Sources: WalkMe, study run in July 2025 among 1,000 US employees (SAP News); Cybernews, 2025 survey of more than 1,000 US employees (Cybernews); Gartner, survey of 302 cybersecurity leaders, March–May 2025 (Gartner).
#ArtificialIntelligence #Leadership #Governance #ShadowAI #EXECIA
Read the full articleabout 3,000 words→
What shadow AI costs, beyond the risks
People mostly talk about leaks and compliance. A quieter cost goes unnoticed: the know-how being built outside the company.
An employee who uses a personal tool every day builds up effective prompts, message templates, ways of working. All of it lives in a private account. The day they leave, that capital leaves with them, without anyone knowing it existed.
Add the scattered spending: individual subscriptions paid with a personal card or slipped into expense claims, often several for the same need. One by one, they look harmless. Added up, they fund an AI policy nobody decided on.
Finally, the company loses negotiating power. Leadership that does not know how many people use which tools can neither choose the right offer nor negotiate its terms.
Which signals show that undeclared use has taken hold?
Without monitoring anyone, a few clues are telling:
subscriptions to AI tools in expense claims or on company cards;
browser extensions or apps installed without going through IT;
documents whose style becomes the same from one department to the next;
sudden gains in speed that nobody explains.
None of these signals calls for a sanction. Each one reveals a need the company has not yet covered.
Which functions are most exposed?
All of them, but not with the same data:
sales, with proposals, price lists, prospect names and the history of exchanges;
human resources, with CVs, appraisals, health or pay information;
finance, with forecasts, margins and unpublished results;
leadership and communications, with reorganisation plans and committee minutes.
A policy becomes clear when it gives, for each function, an example of what can be entrusted to a tool and what never should be.
What does the legal framework say?
Since 2 February 2025, the AI Act, the European AI regulation, has required companies that use AI systems to make sure their people have a sufficient level of AI literacy. Training and informing are no longer just good practice.
The GDPR still applies to any personal data entered into a tool, approved or not. The company remains responsible for what it does with the information of its clients and employees.
The French data protection authority, the CNIL, regularly publishes recommendations on generative AI. They are a solid basis for writing a proportionate policy, without jargon.
How do you choose a business offer rather than a personal account?
Most major vendors offer versions for companies. Their value lies less in the features than in the contractual commitments.
Three questions to ask before signing:
is the data entered used to train the vendor’s models?
where is it hosted, and how long is it kept?
can the company manage the accounts, and close them when an employee leaves?
A clear answer to these three questions is worth more than a long list of features.
Which tools should head the approved list?
The ones that cover the three most frequent needs:
writing or rewording a message;
summarising a long document;
preparing a meeting or a piece of research.
To start, one approved tool per need is enough. More specialised requests, such as data analysis or contract translation, are then handled case by case, with the named contact person.
Do you need a supervised testing space?
Often, yes. A “sandbox” is a space where teams test new tools with fictional or anonymised data, for a limited period.
It answers employees’ legitimate curiosity without exposing the company. And every trial becomes information for leadership: what works, what does not, what deserves approval.
What about contractors and freelancers?
Shadow AI does not stop at your walls. A consultant, an agency or a translator may hand your documents to an AI tool without telling you.
One question before the assignment clears it up: which AI tools will you use, and with which of our information?
A contract clause then sets the rule, just as it already does for confidentiality.
Should employee representatives be involved?
In France, in companies with at least fifty employees, the introduction of new technologies is one of the topics on which the works council is consulted. Rolling out AI tools often falls within that scope.
Beyond the obligation, involving them early has a real advantage: they know the worries on the ground, and they can help you write a policy the teams will accept.
How do you talk about it without worrying teams?
Start with what the company will offer, not with what it will ban. An announcement that opens with “here are the tools you can use from tomorrow” gets heard. One that opens with a list of bans gets worked around.
Then give a single address for questions, with a response time. Trust is earned when a question asked on Monday gets an answer within the week.
What do you do when someone reports a mistake?
Thank them. An employee who reports pasting sensitive information into a tool, or passing on a wrong answer, is doing the company a favour: they make it possible to fix things before the problem grows.
Keep a simple log of these reports, with no names, noting what happened and what changed. After a few months, it becomes the best source for improving the policy. A company that punishes reports stops receiving them, and finds out about its incidents too late.
How do you measure progress?
Four indicators are enough to track the situation from one quarter to the next:
the share of uses declared in the latest review;
the number of people using the approved tools;
the number of questions asked to the contact person;
the average time taken to answer them.
If questions go up, that is a good sign: the rule is known, and teams would rather ask than work around it.
In an SME of twenty people?
The subject looks like something for large groups. Yet it comes up in exactly the same way in a small company, with one advantage: everyone knows each other.
One team meeting is enough to go through the uses. The leader can be the contact person, and the policy fits on one page. What takes months in a group is settled in a few weeks in an SME, as long as you get on with it.
If a client asks you about it?
Some clients are starting to ask their suppliers how they govern AI, especially in security questionnaires and tenders. The question is not about technology. It is about control.
A company that has mapped its uses, approved its tools and written its policy answers in three sentences. One that discovers the question on the day it is asked improvises, and the client can tell.
So all this work also serves a commercial goal: being able to show, with documents to back it up, that you use AI with method. In a market where trust is increasingly on the table, few competitors can present that yet.
A 90-day plan
Three stages, one month each:
from day 1 to day 30, map real uses, starting with the executive committee;
from day 31 to day 60, approve two or three tools that cover the most frequent needs, and write a two-page policy;
from day 61 to day 90, train teams on their own tasks, then measure with the four indicators.
At the end of these three months, the company does not know everything. But it knows what is happening, and it has taken back control.
What shadow AI really reveals
A hidden use is first of all a message: your teams found a gain the company was not offering them. Treating it as a fault means ignoring that message.
Leadership that listens turns a diffuse risk into a roadmap. It knows which needs to cover, which tools to choose and which data to protect first. That is when the AI policy becomes a leadership choice, and no longer a text everyone works around.
Valérie Mailland
Founder of EXEC'IA Consulting. 20+ years alongside executives, including 18 in executive coordination at McKinsey & Company. Follow me on LinkedIn →

## Blog: Not every decision can be delegated
URL : https://exec-ia.ai/perspective-toutes-decisions-ne-se-deleguent-pas-en.html

← All articles ★Blog • Decision
Not every decision
can be delegated.
Not even to an AI.
Article developed from my LinkedIn post (8 September 2026)
Updated on 30 September 2026
Short version →
SME leaders: not every decision can be handed to an AI, however capable.
A simple test: if a decision is easy to undo and its consequences stay limited, you can hand it to AI.
If it is hard to put right, or it commits the company beyond the person who makes it, it stays human.
Air Canada was ordered to honour a promise its own chatbot had made up. Nobody had set the limit beforehand.
The way forward:
write down, once and for all, the short list of decisions you will never hand over to AI.
You run an SME and AI offers you a few more ready-made answers every day?
This piece is for you. I was lucky enough to spend much of my career alongside business leaders. I learned a great deal with them, especially about what makes a decision hard when the data does not all point the same way.
A strategic direction.
A major investment.
A reorganisation.
A decision that affects people.
On paper, these four situations have nothing in common. Yet they share one thing: their consequences reach far beyond the person who decides, and are still felt months, sometimes years later.
A recent Morgan Stanley study on AI governance caught my attention: 41% of the executives surveyed put human oversight of high-risk situations at the top of their governance rules.
To me, that figure is not about distrust. It shows that leaders already sense, instinctively, the difference between what can be delegated and what never should be.
AI can analyse, compare, simulate, shake up an intuition, bring options to light. That is already a lot.
How do you know if a decision can be delegated?
Ask yourself one question: if the decision turns out wrong, can we easily go back?
If yes, and the consequences stay limited, you can hand it to AI without worry. Sorting requests, suggesting a meeting slot, preparing a first summary: mistakes get fixed fast, and nobody is harmed.
If no, because the decision is hard to undo or its effects reach far beyond the person who made it, keep it in human hands. That is not excessive caution. It is in proportion to the risk.
When in doubt, also ask how long it would take to spot a mistake. An error seen in a minute does not call for the same vigilance as one a customer discovers six months later.
⚖️ Why must the final call stay human when a decision commits the company?
What did a real court case reveal about delegating to AI?
In February 2024, a Canadian tribunal ruled on a case that says it all. An Air Canada customer had been promised a refund by the airline’s chatbot. The problem: that promise did not match the company’s policy.
Before the tribunal, Air Canada argued its chatbot was “a separate legal entity that is responsible for its own actions”. The tribunal swept the argument aside: a company answers for what all its agents say, human or automated. Air Canada had to honour the promise.
What strikes me in this story is not the technology. It is that nobody in the company was in charge of checking what the tool could promise on the airline’s behalf. The limit did not exist before the incident. The tribunal set it instead, and not in the most favourable way.
How do you build that list, in practice?
In an SME, it often fits into four families.
One: hiring and dismissal in key roles. A mistake there is rarely repaired without human damage.
Two: commitments made to a client beyond an amount set in advance. That is exactly the chatbot scenario.
Three: decisions that change the company’s course, such as a new offer, a new country or a different business model.
Four: investments above a threshold each leader sets according to the size of the business.
This list does not need to be complete. It needs to exist before the emergency, and be known to everyone who might one day set up an AI tool. A list only the leader carries in their head protects nobody else.
Because a leader does not decide with figures alone. They decide within a context, with a responsibility, and they are the one who lives with the consequences.
Give two leaders exactly the same figures and they may, quite rightly, make opposite decisions. They are not committing the same company, or the same history. No model can carry that share of judgement for the person who will live with the outcome. A model may recommend the same option to both. The leader is the one who answers for the choice.
🎯 Where should the line sit between AI and human decision-making?
AI informs the decision. The leader decides. That limit is not negotiated case by case: it is set once, in a calm moment, before an emergency forces you to improvise.
This is not turning your back on it. It is recognising a simple fact: a tool, however good, will never be the one standing in front of the company to answer for what the decision produced.
The more AI advances, the more knowing what to hand over to it, and what never to hand over, will become a core leadership skill. I am convinced of it.
Is this boundary fixed?
No, and that is good news. A decision that needed human judgement yesterday can, with time and evidence, move over to what a tool handles well on its own: sorting a first level of files, spotting recurring anomalies, preparing a summary.
What does not change is the need to review the limit regularly, instead of setting it once and forgetting it. A limit nobody has reread in two years often describes a world that no longer exists.
So the question I would ask you is not “do you trust AI?”. It is rather: “who, at your company, clearly has the right to say no to what AI recommends?” If the answer is unclear, the limit does not exist yet. It is just assumed.
How do you formalise this boundary?
A short list is enough: the families of decisions the company refuses to hand over to AI, however good the tool. A written list, reread once a year, is worth more than a grand principle everyone reads their own way.
Writing it down has another benefit: it forces you to settle disagreements that, left vague, would only have surfaced at the worst possible moment.
One page is enough, with concrete examples: a dismissal, a price offered to a key client, a commitment to a partner.
Who has the final say when the organisation disagrees?
A list is not enough if nobody knows who has the last word when two trusted people reach opposite conclusions. In a small business, it is often settled by default: the leader decides, and that is fine. The risk comes when the company grows, an executive committee takes shape, and nobody restates clearly who arbitrates.
The answer is nothing complicated. It just needs to be written down, known to everyone, and decided before the disagreement. A company that discovers in the middle of a crisis that it never settled the question settles it in a rush, often badly. Sometimes an AI tool even fills the gap by default. That is exactly the gap the Air Canada case brought to light.
💬 And you, which decision
would you never delegate to an AI?
Source: Morgan Stanley, “AI Governance Survey”, 2026.
#ArtificialIntelligence #Leadership
#Governance #Decision #AIStrategy
Going further
Four more questions to take the thinking further.
Read the full articleabout 3,000 words→
Delegate, assist, decide: three levels to tell apart
The debate is often framed as a choice: let AI decide, or do without it. In real life there are three levels, and most situations play out in the middle.
This is how I describe them:
delegate: the tool acts alone, and someone checks afterwards, from time to time;
assist: the tool prepares, and a person validates before anything happens;
decide: a person makes the call, the tool has only brought information.
For each type of decision, the right question is therefore not “AI or no AI”. It is “at which level”. A single process can even mix all three: an automatic sort, a prepared proposal, then a final human choice.
How do you assess the risk of a decision in a few minutes?
Four questions are enough, to ask before choosing the level:
if the decision is wrong, what happens, and to whom?
how long does it take to notice?
can the mistake be put right, and at what price?
does the decision commit the company to someone else, a customer, an employee or an authority?
The heavier the answers, the more the decision moves back to a person. An error you see at once and fix in a minute has nothing in common with an error a customer discovers six months later.
Who is responsible when an AI gets it wrong?
The company. That is what the Air Canada case recalled, and it is the logic of the law: a tool is responsible for nothing. Whoever uses it to act on their behalf answers for what it produces.
The European AI Act goes further for some uses classed as high-risk, such as recruitment or access to certain essential services. There it requires, among other things, genuine human oversight and informing the people concerned.
For a leader, the consequence is simple: as soon as a tool can commit the company, someone must be named to answer for what it does.
And decisions about people?
Here I would be especially careful. Assessing an employee, turning down a promotion, applying a sanction, choosing between two candidates: these decisions touch someone’s dignity and career.
The GDPR is clear on this: a person has the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, when that decision has legal effects on them or significantly affects them. AI can help prepare, compare, spot something missed. The decision itself stays human, and the person concerned must be able to talk it through with someone.
What does a list look like, in practice?
An example for a service SME of about forty people:
every hire, every termination and every sanction;
every contractual commitment above an amount set by leadership;
every reply to a complaint that admits a fault or promises a goodwill gesture;
every public statement in the company’s name;
every change of prices or commercial terms;
every strategic choice discussed by the executive committee.
Six lines are enough. Each one covers a family of decisions, not a single case: the list stays valid even when the tools change.
Which decisions can you safely hand over to AI?
The ones that tick three boxes:
they come up often, so quality can be checked across many cases;
they follow known rules that can be written down in advance;
a single mistake costs little and is quickly fixed.
Sorting incoming requests, suggesting a meeting slot, flagging an unusual invoice: these decisions often gain from being handed to a tool, with regular checks. They free up time for the ones that deserve a person’s attention.
What if the AI and the expert disagree?
Do not decide too fast, in either direction. The disagreement is information: it reveals either a limit of the tool or a blind spot of the expert.
The most useful move is to ask each side to justify its position. The expert explains what they see that the data does not show. The tool, when asked, says what it relies on. Then the person responsible decides, and writes down what convinced them.
Over time, these recorded disagreements become a goldmine: they show where the tool is reliable, and where human experience remains essential.
And AI agents that act on their own?
Tools no longer just answer. Some send messages, place orders, change files. The question of delegation becomes very concrete.
Before handing an action to an agent, I would put three safeguards in place: a closed list of authorised actions, a ceiling above which human approval is required, and a log that shows who did what, the agent or a person. Without these three safeguards, the company is unknowingly delegating decisions it never chose.
The automation trap
A recommendation shown with confidence tends to be followed, even by competent people. The more often the tool is right, the more attention drops, and the more the rare mistake slips through.
You do not fight this with suspicion. You fight it with organisation. Rotating the people who review, setting a maximum number of approvals per day, rechecking an already approved file now and then: these simple habits keep attention where it matters.
How do you involve teams in drawing the line?
By asking them what they would never delegate. The people dealing with customers, suppliers or files know better than anyone where a mistake is costly.
A one-hour workshop, where everyone names a decision from their daily work and the level they would give it, often reveals risks leadership had not seen. And the teams feel, rightly, that the rule was built with them.
How do you train managers in this judgement?
With cases rather than principles. A manager learns more from looking at three real situations, where the tool was right, wrong or half right, than from reading a policy note.
It can become a short ritual in management meetings: one case a month, one simple question, “at which level would you have placed this decision?”. Judgement is built that way, through practice, like any leadership skill.
How do you talk about it with the board or the partners?
With a map rather than a speech. A table listing the main types of decisions, the level chosen for each and the person responsible answers most questions before anyone asks them.
Partners and board members are not asking the company to give up AI. They want to know that someone has thought about the limits, and that those limits are respected.
How do you review the line over time?
Once a year, with facts. For each type of delegated or assisted decision, look at the number of errors found, how serious they were and how long it took to spot them.
If errors are rare and minor, the decision can move down a level. If a serious error has appeared, it moves back up, long enough to understand what happened. The line stays alive, grounded in experience rather than the mood of the moment.
What this line says about a leadership team
Writing down what you do not delegate forces you to say what matters. It is an exercise in clear thinking as much as in caution.
A leadership team that knows where to draw the line can use AI more boldly everywhere else. Being clear about a few protected decisions frees up use on all the others.
How do you document a decision made with the help of an AI?
→
Keep a record of three things: the question asked, the options you looked at, and the reason for your choice. That short account lets you reread the decision later and understand what weighed.
No need to turn it into a file. A few lines written on the spot are worth more than a reconstruction after the fact. A paragraph in the meeting notes is often enough.
Add a fourth thing: what the AI had suggested and you did not keep. That is often where real judgement shows. It is also what an auditor or a client will ask you for first.
What does real human oversight consist of?
→
You need someone who reviews, at a precise moment, with the power to say no. Reviewing for form’s sake, with no power to stop anything, is not oversight. It is a signature.
The right question: at your company, who can turn down an AI recommendation, and under what conditions?
That person also needs the time to do it. A sign-off requested at the end of the day, across dozens of files, always ends up as a simple approval click. If you want real oversight, plan the time that goes with it.
How do you teach teams to challenge a recommendation?
→
Give them three questions. What does this recommendation rest on?
What could make it wrong?
What happens if we get it wrong?
They take five minutes to learn and work for everything.
With them, the AI’s answer becomes the start of the thinking, no longer its conclusion.
Practise on past cases whose ending you know. The team then sees where the AI would have been wrong, and learns to spot its blind spots without taking any risk.
After a few sessions, these questions become a team reflex rather than an instruction.
What place should be left for the leader’s intuition?
→
A real one, as long as you say it out loud. Intuition is often years of experience summed up in a second. Setting it aside in the name of data would be as questionable as following it without looking at the figures.
AI informs, intuition warns, and the leader decides, owning the choice.
A habit I like: write down your intuition before consulting the AI. A few weeks later, compare. You will learn a lot about how reliable each one is.
It is also the best way to learn when to listen to it.
Valérie Mailland
Founder of EXEC'IA Consulting. 20+ years alongside executives, including 18 in executive coordination at McKinsey & Company. Follow me on LinkedIn →

## AI transformation rarely fails
URL : https://exec-ia.ai/perspective-transformation-echoue-rarement-technologie-en.html

← All articles Blog • Transformation
AI transformation rarely fails
because of the technology.
It fails when the organisation
has not changed, only the tool.
Article developed from my LinkedIn post (9 September 2026)
Updated on 1 October 2026
Short version →
SME leaders: AI transformation rarely fails because of the technology.
According to a 2026 Orgvue survey, 78% of organisations have seen AI projects fail or stall at pilot stage. The cause: a lack of alignment with the organisation, not a lack of tools.
A real transformation touches three things, in this order: who decides, which processes are redesigned, which roles change.
The sign it has not happened: there are still just as many approval meetings.
To get started, one page is enough: who will need to decide differently once the tool is in place?
If the answer is “no one”, you are automating what already exists. You are transforming nothing.
You run an SME and you are launching an AI project?
This piece is for you. During my years alongside business leaders, I saw plenty of tools and transformation plans come and go. AI did not yet exist in this form. But the story was already the same.
The tool is rarely the problem. The problem is everything that does not move around it.
We saw it with every technology wave: ERP systems in the 2000s, then CRM, then the cloud more recently. Each time, the tool kept its technical promises. Each time, some of the companies that adopted it got only a fraction of the promised value, because nothing else had changed around it.
A RAND Corporation report cites an estimate worth pausing on: more than 80% of AI projects fail. The reason is not technical: these projects are not aligned with the company’s priorities and organisation.
A survey published in May 2026 confirms it. Among 1,163 senior decision-makers in eight countries, Orgvue found that 78% of organisations have seen AI projects fail or stall at pilot stage. Its chief executive puts these failures down to how work is organised, not to the technology.
That figure does not mean AI does not work.
It means a tool, on its own, transforms nothing.
🔧 Why is changing the software not enough?
Because you keep the same processes, the same roles, the same meetings where nobody decides.
The result: AI is added on top of what exists. It does not change it.
The surest sign that no transformation happened?
There are still just as many approval meetings. A new tool that goes through exactly the same approval circuit, with the same people consulted in the same order, has transformed nothing. It sped up one link. The chain is just as long as before.
Have economists already named this pattern?
Yes, and for a long time. Back in 1987, economist Robert Solow observed, about the computerisation of companies: “You can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics.” Researchers Erik Brynjolfsson and Lorin Hitt later showed why. Technology only pays off when it comes with an equivalent investment in the organisation, often invisible in budgets: redesigning processes, redistributing decisions, evolving roles.
Generative AI is doing exactly the same thing, only faster. The tool is installed in a few weeks. The organisation takes months, sometimes years, to follow, when it follows at all. That gap is what the estimate cited by RAND shows: only one project in five would cross it successfully.
What does this mean concretely for a mid-sized company’s leader?
A very direct consequence: the budget for an AI project should never stop at the licence and the technical integration. Keep part of it for the time you will spend with the teams working out who decides what, once the tool is in place. That time appears on no supplier invoice. Yet it is what decides whether your project joins the four in five that fail, or the fifth that succeeds.
Six months after launch, run a simple test. Ask the team to describe how they work without mentioning the tool. If the description matches the old one line for line, with one extra step, nothing has been transformed. The software changed. The work did not.
🎯 What three things does a real AI transformation have to touch?
Who decides, and when.
Which processes are rethought, not just automated.
Which roles genuinely evolve.
If the decision stays at the same level as before, automating only speeds up a bottleneck that was already there. Doing a useless step faster does not make it useful. If nobody changes what they do with the time saved, that time fills up with something else, with no gain for the company. These three points are checked one by one: you can automate without deciding differently, or decide differently without any role changing. Either way, one is missing to call it a transformation.
Without these three changes, the company quickly slips back into its old habits, with one more tool.
In what order should you tackle these three points?
The order matters. First, who decides and when: until that is clear, nobody knows which process to redesign first. Then the process. Then the roles. A role does not change because someone announced it would. It changes because the actual work has changed shape.
Starting at the end, by announcing that roles will change without having redesigned either the decision or the process, rarely gives the result you hoped for. The message changes, and the results stay the same.
Where should you start, concretely?
Before any AI project, do not ask what the tool will do. Ask who will need to decide differently once it is in place. If the answer is “no one”, you are automating what exists, not transforming anything.
That map fits on one page. Its shortness is exactly what makes it impossible to dodge. Do it in an hour, with the heads of the teams concerned: for each decision the tool touches, write down who makes it today, who will make it tomorrow, and when.
How can you quickly tell where your organisation stands?
Three questions are usually enough to see where an AI project stands. Answer them honestly, with the team that uses the tool every day, not only with the person who chose it. The gap between the two sets of answers is often a finding in itself.
Has anyone, since rollout, made a decision they would not have made before, with the same authority as before?
Has a process lost a step, rather than gained one?
Has anyone seen their role redefined, not just their tool?
If you answer no three times, the project stands a good chance of joining the four in five that fail, according to the estimate cited by RAND, however good the chosen AI is. The reverse holds too: three yeses mean the company has started to change, even if the tool itself is modest.
This test does not replace a full diagnosis. But it takes ten minutes, needs no consultant, and tells you straight away whether the topic deserves a closer look. It is the first question I would ask about an AI project already under way: not “which tool did you choose?”, but “who, at your company, decides differently since it went live?”.
💬 In your organisation,
what should change before the tool, not after?
Sources: RAND Corporation, “The Root Causes of Failure for Artificial Intelligence Projects and How They Can Succeed”, 2024; Orgvue, “92% of organizations have invested in AI but 78% say projects have either stalled or failed”, 12 May 2026.
#ArtificialIntelligence #Transformation #Leadership #Organisation #AIStrategy
Going further
Four more questions to take the thinking further.
Read the full articleabout 3,000 words→
How is generative AI different from earlier waves?
On one point, it changes everything: it comes in through employees, not through leadership. An ERP or a CRM was rolled out from the top, with a project, a budget and a timeline. A generative AI tool is downloaded in two minutes, without asking anyone.
So transformation no longer starts from a plan. It starts from uses that already exist, often invisible, which leadership must first discover before it can steer them. It is not only the speed that changes: it is the starting point.
Why does productivity often dip before it rises?
Because a company that changes the way it works first pays a learning cost. Economists, including Erik Brynjolfsson, call this a J-curve: performance dips while teams learn and processes are reorganised, then climbs above where it started.
Knowing this curve avoids a common mistake: stopping a project at the bottom of the dip, just when the effort is starting to pay off. Announce the dip in advance, with its likely length: you also protect the teams’ trust.
Which process should you start with?
The one that ticks four boxes:
it comes up often, every day or every week;
it frustrates people, those who do it and those waiting for the result;
its result is visible, to a client or to leadership;
it only involves one or two teams.
A first success on a process like that is worth more than an ambitious project that gets bogged down. It brings proof, and proof makes people want to continue elsewhere.
Should you automate first, then transform?
Starting by automating one step is not a mistake, as long as you do it knowingly. Automation lets you learn, measure and reassure.
The mistake is stopping there. With every automation, ask one question in writing: if this step goes faster, which decision or which next step must change for the gain to reach the client?
Without that question, you pile up local speed-ups that never join together.
How do you handle the period when old and new run side by side?
By giving it an end date. Keeping the old process next to the new one reassures people at first, then becomes the worst of both worlds: everyone does their work twice, and nobody knows which version counts.
A switchover date, known to everyone, settles the question. Before that date, the old process remains the reference. After it, only the new one counts, and the old one disappears, including the files and shortcuts that would let people quietly go back to it.
An example: handling quotes in an SME
Before the project, a quote follows this circuit:
the salesperson gathers the information and writes a first draft;
the technical lead checks it is feasible;
leadership approves the price;
the assistant formats and sends it.
An AI tool can prepare the first draft in a few minutes. If the rest of the circuit does not change, the quote simply waits longer at the next step.
The real transformation is asking, for example, whether leadership needs to approve every price, or only those outside an agreed grid. And whether the technical check can rely on a checklist prepared by the tool. The gain comes from those two decisions far more than from faster drafting.
What new roles are emerging?
Not necessarily new jobs, but new responsibilities. Better to name them than to leave them floating.
Three come up often:
the go-to person, who knows the tool and answers colleagues’ questions;
the reviewer, who checks what the tool produces before it leaves the team;
the process owner, who decides how the circuit evolves and settles things when two teams disagree.
These responsibilities take time. If they are added without taking anything else away, they are done badly, then not at all.
Which skills should come first?
Less technical skill than three core abilities: saying clearly what you expect, checking what you get, and judging when the result is not right.
These skills are nothing new. They belong to anyone who knows how to delegate: hand over a task, check the result, take back control if needed. Managers who already have them adapt quickly to AI tools. Those who never developed them discover the problem at that point.
How do you measure that a transformation is moving forward?
Four simple indicators say more than a complicated dashboard:
the time between a request and the decision that answers it;
the number of steps in the processes concerned;
the share of teams actually using the new tools;
the time freed up, and what it is used for.
Recorded at launch and then every quarter, these figures tell the real story of the project, far better than impressions shared in meetings.
How do you stop the project resting on one person?
Many transformations have an engine: an enthusiastic person who found the tool, convinced leadership and trained colleagues. The day that person changes jobs, the project fades out.
The fix: form a pair early on, then a small group, sharing knowledge and decisions. Writing down what you have learned, the instructions that work, the mistakes to avoid, is as much part of the project as the rollout itself.
Should you tell your clients?
Yes, as soon as the transformation changes something for them: a lead time, a contact person, the format of an answer. A client who has been told accepts an adjustment. A client who is surprised sees it as a step backwards.
Ask them for their opinion a few weeks after the switchover. You will get a measure your internal indicators cannot give: has the change improved their experience, or only the company’s?
How long should you allow?
Longer than rolling out the tool, and less time than you fear if you go step by step. On a limited process, a few months are often enough to see the decision, the circuit and the roles move.
What stretches timelines is rarely the technology. It is the decisions that keep being postponed: who approves now, which step disappears, who takes over which task. Every week of delay is paid for in double work and weary teams.
What do you tell teams about what will not change?
It is often the most awaited question, and the least addressed. A transformation worries people because it seems to call everything into question.
Say clearly what stays the same: the values, the commitments to clients, the people you report to. You give those who must change the rest something to hold on to. Change goes down better when it has known limits.
When should you bring in an outside view?
When the company can no longer see its own habits. Approval circuits, ritual meetings and unwritten roles seem natural to those who live them every day.
An outside view does not bring a ready-made solution. It asks the questions nobody asks internally any more, with no power at stake, and helps separate what is necessary from what is only habit.
What transformation really demands
Leadership time, more than budget. Tools can be bought quickly. Decisions about who decides, which processes change and which roles evolve cannot be delegated.
Leadership that agrees to give that time gets what no tool will ever give on its own: a company that works differently, not just faster.
How do you involve teams from the start?
→
Get them involved in describing the problem, before anyone talks about a solution. The people doing the work know the real sticking points, the ones no organisation chart shows.
A transformation built with them is far more likely to be applied than one that is simply announced.
A half-day workshop, where everyone describes a painful task from their week, often brings out more ideas than a questionnaire.
Invite an open sceptic too. Their objections, heard early, cost far less than resistance discovered after launch.
In practice: a one-hour workshop with four or five people from the field, and a single question: “what makes you lose the most time?”
How do you know an organisation has really changed?
→
Three concrete signs. Decisions are made by other people, or at another time. Processes have changed in practice. Roles have evolved, and some tasks have been dropped.
If none of that has moved, the tool is installed, but the company has not changed.
It is easier to see with someone outside the day-to-day, who asks naive questions with no power at stake.
Ask the question again a few months later. Real change lasts. Cosmetic change fades as soon as attention drops.
A simple test: ask a newcomer how things work here. If they describe the old way of doing things, nothing has really changed.
What do you do when the transformation stalls?
→
Go back to the starting question: what was supposed to change, and what is blocking it?
The answer is almost always a decision not taken, a process not redesigned or a role not clarified.
Adding a tool at that point makes the problem worse. First remove the obstacle within the organisation.
A short check-in, once a month, on the obstacle of the moment is enough to stop the blockage from settling in.
Write the obstacle down in black and white, with an owner and a date. A blockage nobody owns ends up worked around rather than removed.
A checkpoint every two weeks is enough to see whether the obstacle has moved.
What role does the leader play over time?
→
Holding the course, and making the choices visible: what continues, what stops, what we will not do. A transformation lasts months, and the leader’s attention is one of its scarcest resources.
A leader who stays present, without steering everything, gives the company permission to change.
It is also a signal: the topic remains a leadership priority, not a project quietly fading away.
A few minutes set aside for the topic at every executive committee meeting are enough to keep that signal alive.
The strongest signal is still the example: a leader who applies the new way of working themselves is worth every speech.
Valérie Mailland
Founder of EXEC'IA Consulting. 20+ years alongside executives, including 18 in executive coordination at McKinsey & Company. Follow me on LinkedIn →

The AI budget is not the issue. Buy-in is.
An AI policy that its own leaders do not follow is no longer a policy.

## AI CV screening: who rereads the rejected applications?
URL : https://exec-ia.ai/perspective-tri-cv-ia-candidatures-ecartees-en.html

← All articles Blog • Recruitment
AI CV screening: who rereads
the rejected applications?
7 October 2026 · Updated on October 7, 2026
Short version →
Business leaders, HR directors, hiring managers: software that screens your CVs puts your responsibility on the line.
In the United States, candidates rejected by Workday’s tool are seeking a class action. In France, the data-protection authority CNIL has made recruitment an inspection priority for 2026.
The EU AI Act classifies CV screening as high-risk, with obligations from 2 December 2027.
Three checks before any rollout: the training data, the review of rejected applications, and the explanation of a rejection.
Do you recruit, run HR or sign off on hires?
Software may already be sorting your applications, sometimes without anyone having really decided it.
This article helps you understand what it does, and what you answer for.
🎯 What does CV screening software do?
It reads applications for you, compares them with the job and ranks them. Applicant tracking systems, often called ATS, look for keywords, assign a score and automatically reject certain profiles. Many now build in AI to “understand” a career path.
The time saved is real. So is the risk: a candidate rejected by the machine is, most of the time, never read by anyone.
What is the Workday case?
Derek Mobley, an African-American candidate over 40, accuses Workday’s screening tool of rejecting him for dozens of jobs. He is not suing the employers one by one: he is going after the software vendor, which he holds responsible for the screening.
The case is moving forward, step by step:
May 2025: the judge grants preliminary certification of a collective action for candidates over 40;
22 June 2026: she largely denies the motion to dismiss;
September 2026: the plaintiffs seek class certification on behalf of four groups, Black applicants, women, people over 40 and people with disabilities;
9 March 2027: the hearing date on that motion.
The stakes go well beyond one candidate. According to a Workday witness, more than 356 million applications went through the tool in 2024.
Why can an algorithm discriminate?
Because it learns from the past. An algorithm trained on ten years of hiring reproduces the choices, and the blind spots, of the people who hired before it.
The best-known example comes from Amazon. In 2018, Reuters revealed that the company had dropped an experimental CV screening tool: trained on mostly male hires, it penalised applications that included the word “women’s”.
And in France?
The CNIL has made recruitment one of its inspection priorities for 2026. It checks three points: the use of automated screening, the information given to candidates, and how long their data is kept. It starts with large companies and recruitment firms. The rules, however, apply to everyone.
French labour law already sets the principle: candidates must be told, before they are used, which recruitment methods and techniques are applied to them.
What does the AI Act change?
The EU regulation classifies AI systems used to recruit, filter applications or assess candidates as high-risk systems. Human oversight, documentation, informing the people concerned: these obligations will apply from 2 December 2027.
They do not target only the vendor. The employer using the tool will have duties of its own.
🎯 Three checks before handing your CVs to AI:
What data did the tool learn from?
Who rereads the rejected applications, not just the shortlisted ones?
Can you explain to a candidate why they were turned down?
AI sorts faster. It does not judge more fairly. The decision to reject someone remains a human decision, even when a machine carries it out.
💬 In your company,
who rereads what the algorithm rejects?
Sources: Lawyer Monthly, 21 September 2026; Duane Morris, 25 September 2026; summary of the 2026 rulings (Refonte Learning); Légisocial, CNIL 2026 inspections; French Labour Code, articles L1221-6, L1221-8 and L1221-9; Reuters, 10 October 2018.
#EXECIA #ArtificialIntelligence #Recruitment #Governance #AIAct
Read the full articleabout 3,000 words→
How does automated screening work?
Recruitment software usually performs three steps. First, it extracts information from the CV: degrees, jobs, dates, skills. Then it compares that information with the job ad, often by keywords or by similarity of meaning. Finally, it assigns a score and ranks applications, sometimes with knock-out questions asked directly in the form.
Each of these steps can rule out a strong profile. A CV with an unusual layout is misread. An unusual job title matches no keyword. A clumsy answer to a knock-out question closes the door, without any human ever seeing it.
The most common blind spots
Some profiles are rejected more often than others, without anyone intending it:
careers with a gap, for parental leave, illness or a personal project;
career changers, whose skills do not carry the expected words;
older candidates, given away by their graduation dates;
people trained abroad, whose qualifications are poorly recognised;
applications written without the sector’s codes.
For an SME struggling to hire, this is a paradox: the tool meant to widen the talent pool can shrink it to profiles that all look alike. Hard-to-fill jobs are precisely those where unusual career paths matter most.
When AI reads CVs written by AI
Candidates use AI too. They tailor their CV to each ad, reuse the keywords from the posting, and polish a perfect cover letter in seconds. Recruiters know the result: more applications, smoother ones, harder to tell apart.
Faced with this sameness, the temptation is to sort even faster and even more automatically. That is the wrong reflex. The more documents look alike, the more valuable human judgement becomes to spot what makes the difference: real experience, motivation, the ability to learn.
Why the issue is arriving now
Three trends are converging. Applications are multiplying, because applying now takes only minutes. Screening tools are becoming standard, often switched on by default in job boards and HR software. And the authorities are stepping in: the CNIL inspects, the AI Act sets a deadline, US courts rule.
For a business leader, the question is no longer “should we use AI to recruit?”. It is already there, inside the tools. The question becomes: “who in our company knows what it does?”.
What AI does well in recruitment
Used well, AI saves precious time without deciding for you:
writing a clear job ad, free of jargon and discriminatory wording;
summarising a long career to prepare an interview;
suggesting interview questions tied to the real skills of the job;
scheduling interviews and replying quickly to every candidate.
In all these uses, a person keeps control of the decision. That is the line to hold: AI prepares, people decide.
Knock-out questions: the hidden trap
Many forms ask yes-or-no questions that reject automatically: driving licence, immediate availability, years of experience. One answer does not match, and the application disappears. Nobody sees it.
Review these questions one by one. Are they truly essential to the job? Does four years of experience instead of five justify never meeting someone? In many SMEs, removing two knock-out questions is enough to reopen the pool.
What French law already says
The French Labour Code sets three simple principles. Information requested from a candidate may only be used to assess their ability to do the job. Candidates must be told which recruitment methods and techniques are applied to them. No information about them may be collected by a system they have not been told about.
The principle of non-discrimination applies at every stage of recruitment, including automated screening. And Article 22 of the GDPR gives everyone the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing when it significantly affects them. A hiring rejection decided by a machine, with no real human involvement, falls within that scope.
What the AI Act will require from employers
From 2 December 2027, a company using a high-risk tool will have to use it according to the vendor’s instructions, assign oversight to competent people, monitor how it works and keep its logs for at least six months.
It will also have to inform workers’ representatives and affected employees before putting such a system into service at work, and inform the people subject to its decisions. A rejected candidate will be able to ask for an explanation of the role the tool played. These obligations should be prepared now, when choosing software, not the day before the deadline.
What other countries already do
Since July 2023, New York City has required employers using automated employment decision tools to commission an annual bias audit, publish a summary of the results and notify candidates. Other US states have adopted or are preparing similar rules.
The logic is converging on both sides of the Atlantic: an employer cannot hide behind its vendor. It must know what the tool does, measure it and be able to answer for it.
Six questions to ask a vendor
Before signing, these questions save months:
what data was the model trained on, and how recent is it?
which criteria drive the score, and can we see them?
has the tool undergone a bias audit, and by whom?
can automatic rejection be switched off, keeping a simple ranking?
where is candidate data stored, and for how long?
how is the tool preparing for the AI Act obligations?
A serious vendor answers in writing. If it dodges, you know what its promise of objectivity is worth.
What the rejected candidate goes through
They send an application one evening and receive an automatic rejection minutes later, sometimes in the middle of the night. They realise no human read it. They will never know why.
Multiply that experience by dozens of applications, and you get discouraged people, sometimes among the most experienced. That is exactly what the plaintiff in the Workday case describes. For a company, it is also a reputational risk: a rejection that feels mechanical gets talked about, online and offline.
Four indicators to track
Without complicated tools, four figures show whether screening stays under control:
the share of applications rejected without any human reading;
the number of profiles recovered during the monthly review;
the time taken to reply to candidates, rejections included;
requests for review or explanation received, and what followed.
A four-line table, updated monthly, is enough. It shows leadership what the tool is doing, and it is evidence of diligence the day someone asks the question.
Train the people who hire
The AI Act requires oversight to be assigned to people with the necessary competence and authority. For an SME, that means something simple: hiring managers must know how to read a score, understand the settings and dare to recover a profile.
Half a day is often enough: understanding how the tool ranks, spotting its blind spots, practising on a few rejected applications. It is a small investment compared with the cost of a bad hire or a good candidate lost.
Rereading the rejected: a simple method
Rereading every rejected application would wipe out the time saved. Rereading a sample is enough to stay in control. Every month, one person randomly picks one rejected application in ten and reads it in full.
They ask a single question: “would I have wanted to meet this candidate?”. If the answer is often yes, the tool rejects too much, or wrongly. The settings must change. This check takes an hour a month. It turns a black box into a tool you actually steer.
Measuring without profiling
To find out whether the tool disadvantages a group, you need to compare pass rates from one stage to the next. In France, collecting certain data, such as ethnic origin, is prohibited: the point is not to profile candidates.
You can, however, compare what you already know legitimately: the share of applications from women and men, age bands inferred from careers, career changers, careers with gaps. If one category almost vanishes after screening, that is a signal to examine, with the vendor and, if needed, with a lawyer.
The role of the hiring manager
Hiring managers know the job. They know a good technician can come from another sector, and that a salesperson changing careers brings a valuable network. Involve them in setting up the tool and in reviewing rejections: they see at once when the machine misses something.
Give them the right to recover a profile, too. A tool that does not let you overturn an automatic rejection is not an assistant: it is a filter nobody controls any more.
What you owe candidates
One clear sentence in your job ads and acknowledgement emails is enough to start: “we use a tool to help screen applications; any rejected application can be reviewed by a person on request”. That transparency meets the Labour Code and reassures.
It also protects your reputation. A candidate rejected without explanation talks about it. A candidate who knows a human can review their file keeps a good opinion of the company, even after a rejection. In a market where hiring is hard, that reputation counts.
What if a candidate challenges a decision?
They can ask which data was used, how their application was handled and whether an automated decision was made. They can complain to the CNIL or, if they believe they faced discrimination, to France’s rights ombudsman, the Défenseur des droits.
The best answer is prepared before the complaint: written criteria, a record of reviews, and someone able to explain the rejection in plain words. With those three elements, a challenge becomes a conversation. Without them, it becomes a case file.
And small businesses?
An SME does not receive thousands of applications. But it often uses screening features built into job boards or payroll and HR software without knowing it. The first step is to check which automatic screening features are switched on in these tools, and who switched them on.
For a few dozen applications per job, assisted ranking followed by a human read remains the best approach. AI can summarise, compare and prepare interview questions. It does not need to decide who gets an interview.
Video interviews analysed by AI
Some tools promise to analyse a candidate’s facial expressions or tone of voice during a video interview. In Europe, the AI Act has banned emotion recognition systems in the workplace since 2 February 2025, except for medical or safety reasons. Recruitment falls within that scope.
If a vendor offers you this kind of feature, the answer is simple: no. It exposes the company to penalties, and it judges candidates on signals that have nothing to do with their skills.
Who is responsible: the vendor or the employer?
In the United States, the Workday case is testing a new idea: the software vendor could be held liable as an agent acting for the employer. In Europe, the AI Act already divides the roles: the provider answers for the tool’s design, the employer using it answers for how it is used.
Either way, the employer cannot get off the hook by saying “it was the software”. Set out in the contract what the vendor guarantees: bias audits, documentation, support during an inspection. And keep a record of your own settings.
An assisted-recruitment charter, in four lines
One page is enough, shared with the managers who hire:
no application is rejected without a human being able to review it;
screening criteria are written down and tied to the job;
a sample of rejections is reviewed every month;
any candidate can ask for a review and an explanation.
This charter costs nothing. It will serve you on the day of an inspection, a complaint or a simple question from a candidate.
A typical example
Take a manufacturing company of eighty people looking for a maintenance technician. The job board it uses offers automatic screening, switched on by default. In three weeks, forty applications come in; nine are passed to the recruiter.
The HR manager rereads four rejected applications. Among them is a former truck mechanic changing careers, rejected for lacking the right degree title. He is interviewed, then hired. The company switches off automatic rejection and keeps a simple ranking. Screening takes a little longer; hiring takes much less.
My advice to a business leader
A five-step method, without waiting for 2027:
list the tools already screening your applications, including features switched on by default;
ask each vendor the six questions and keep their answers in writing;
replace automatic rejection with ranking wherever possible;
reread a sample of rejected applications every month;
inform candidates clearly and offer them a human review.
None of these steps requires a budget. They require one named person to be responsible for screening, and to have the time to do it.
Hiring remains a leadership decision. AI can prepare, compare and summarise. It must never decide a candidate’s fate on its own.
Valérie Mailland
Founder of EXEC'IA Consulting. 20+ years alongside executives, including 18 in executive coordination at McKinsey & Company. Follow me on LinkedIn →
